(Part 2: Supplementary – for those rare few who actually care. Once again, my greatest apologies for having to resort to double-posting.)

Chika and Yumi form what I call one of the three “mask pairs” among the twenty main girls, because – you guessed it – all six of those characters are defined by their apparent image not matching with who they truly are inside, though the reason for that disconnect is different between each pair. In Chika’s and Yumi’s case, it all goes back to my aforementioned point about stereotypes, because both of them wear masks that were put on them by *others*, and are simply so used to being “judged by their cover” that they don’t even bother trying to correct those constantly arising misunderstandings, unless they are made by someone close to their personal circle: people who Chika and Yumi strongly *want to* be understood by. The common theme here is both girls being defined through their surface-level appearances and relationships with their peers, except that one of them is extremely social, thriving on constant public validation, while the other is extremely anti-social and couldn’t care less what the outside world (with a few select exceptions) thinks of her – same core foundation, diametrically opposite approach.

Ayane and Sana are the second “mask pair”, though unlike the previous girls these two wear their masks completely of their own volition, as a way to deal with personal issues.

Ayane is a “fake it till you make it” kind of gal who desperately wishes to become this “perfect wife/mother” figure, but the truth of it all is that underneath the mature front Ayane constantly puts up she is *still* just a frightened teenager who is not yet capable of bearing such a burden, neither physically nor mentally. Sana’s mask, on the other hand, is (or, well, was) more of an adaptive defense mechanism than anything else: she is a seedling of an exotic flower who grew up in a climate completely unfit for someone like her, and so she ended up appearing unassuming – not because Sana *actually is* that way, but simply due to her stunted growth: acting shy and timid helped her survive and adapt to her surroundings. And, consequently, once the conditions (artificially, thanks to HOPE) changed to instead be *conductive* to her proper development, Sana quickly blossomed and revealed her true colors: dark, disturbing and poisonous.

So both girls ultimately become closer to their “true selves” over the course of the story, just one of them does it by growing *into* her mask, while the other grows *out of* it. And, as a secondary common link, the Venn diagram for Ayane and Sana also revolves around the subject of “family”: Ayane grew up in a mostly neglectful household and has a strong yearning for a family of her own, while Sana grew up with a mother who deeply cared and sacrificed everything for her, only to repay that love and sacrifice with cruel and callous disregard.

Makoto and Miku are united by their single-minded obsession with the main (and only) thing they excel at: the thing they initially focused their entire life around, but then eventually moved away from once they lost their main motivation and/or discovered something else that brings them just as much joy. Both girls are also extremely competitive, goal-driven, used to being in leadership roles, have deep-rooted self-esteem issues (Makoto’s feelings of not being appreciated due to everything she does as a class representative and Akira’s unofficial secretary, and Miku’s complex regarding her own femininity) in addition to some traumatic childhood experience that is in some way related to their parents – experience that both girls are fundamentally defined by and desperately try to hide from others.

As for the juxtaposition, there is a surface-level contrast of “very smart vs very dumb” and “intellectual vs physical” in terms of their main specializations, plus the girls’ respective histories with the subject of sex: one literally grew up around it, the other had no idea how babies are made before Sensei “corrupted” her – though, despite these differences, Makoto and Miku both end up having very high libidos, sharing the same lack of self-control and disregard towards potential consequences whenever they get horny enough.

For Rin and Futaba, their similarity lies in the hidden darkness they both carry within themselves – darkness that only reveals itself occasionally, creating a striking contrast to the girls’ usual optimistic and kind-hearted demeanor, and also shares the same two common elements: firstly, it is always directed inward, not outward, only manifesting in self-destructive ways (like Rin’s cutting or Futaba’s bulimia) rather than hurting others; and secondly, both girls are fundamentally unable to ever actually *get rid of* that darkness (for one reason or another), and so they are instead forced to live with it and learn how to deal with that suffocating curse on a day-to-day basis, simply managing its symptoms rather than raising their hopes for a more permanent solution.

The juxtaposition here, likewise, lies in how the girls’ “episodes” cause a drastic switch in their usual personalities, making them act in similarly uncharacteristic but equally opposing ways, like a direct reversal of their regular selves: normally cheerful and energetic Rin completely shuts down and becomes entirely apathetic towards everything, while normally calm and gentle Futaba becomes a cornered animal who blindly lashes out in anger against anyone who dares to approach her.

Ami and Maya are the third and final “mask pair”, completing the thematic trifecta of “man vs self” and “man vs society” with “man vs God” – or, well, “man vs (ever-repeating) world”, to be more precise (there is a “Sekai” pun to be made somewhere in there). The specifics of how the fake fronts these two put up were directly caused by the supernatural circumstances they found themselves in is something that I already talked about at length in my earlier Ami analysis, so I won’t repeat any of it here.

I will, however, mention another similarity between Room 5 girls, besides their obvious and uncontested meta-relevance: the fact that both Ami and Maya have zero qualms with effectively objectifying themselves when it comes to their relationship with Sensei. Every other character in the game wants to either be treated as an equal romantic partner by him (basically 85% of the cast) or to arrange some kind of “quid pro quo” deal with the guy that is less about feelings and more about raw mutual benefits (Sana and Haruka, mainly, plus Nodoka/Otoha, Tsubasa and a few potential others), yet *those two* have consistently went above and beyond by repeatedly basing their entire personal value on one thing and one thing only: how their existence can directly benefit Akira. Neither girl particularly minds being treated like a “tool” rather than an independent individual, as long as *he* is the one using them – though, of course, the principle of juxtaposition applies here, as well: with “caretaker” Ami being externally selfless and internally selfish, and “cumdump” Maya being externally selfish and internally selfless.

Molly and Tsuneyo are both eccentric weirdoes who aren’t loners by nature (unlike Nodoka, for example), but still have great difficulty properly fitting in with their peers, causing them to mostly just seek companionship in each other. Both girls also share the same mindset of treating their inherent weirdness as something to be proud of *as well as* a severe personal flaw: being perfectly content with who they are and not desire change, while also having an objective understanding of all of the ways this “strangeness” negatively affects their daily lives, needlessly complicating things that should just be second nature and instead transforming them into difficult puzzles with no clear solutions – the main difference, of course, being that Molly *chose* to be like this, while Tsuneyo had this *chosen for her*.

Finally, another trait that the two of them have in common (besides being extremely passionate about their hobbies) is the their strong personal affinity towards one of their parents: Molly takes after her mom, Tsuneyo follows in the footsteps of her dad – both of whom passed down a lot of cultural/ideological heritage to their daughters (heritage that the girls now deeply respect and appreciate, using it as a conduit to better connect with said parent), and also have a strong association with death: the latter is already one foot in the grave, and the former took her own life.

Uta and Io are perhaps the most obvious duo in terms of what theme they embody, and there is not much I can say about them that hasn’t already been directly said by the game itself. Both girls got involved in a sexual relationship of some kind at a very young age, which then directly intersects which another common point they share: “family” – except that, obviously, for one of them family is something that you deeply love and cherish (and that deeply loves and cherishes you back), while for the other “family” was the sole source of her misfortune. Their reactions to this shared trauma are also diametrically opposed: Uta is an affection-craving nymphomaniac with zero impulse control, and Io is… well, Io – no further elaboration necessary.

Nodoka and Otoha are both “geniuses” in their own fields who also share the exact same occasional bouts of creative mania, but the thing I’d like to highlight the most about these two is the fact that, in many ways, they both serve as direct mirrors to each other:

Nodoka is a character who, right from the get-go, presents herself to be about as strange and incomprehensible as an actual eldritch monstrosity featured in the story (Nao-chan): the girl boasts a frankly absurd level of memory and intelligence, makes constant references to parallel worlds stacked on top of each other (or some other bullshit), implies that she was “created, not born”, constantly speaks to strange girl(s) that visit her in her dreams, and just in general acts borderline inhuman. And yet, ever since the events of 0.44-0.45, we have been getting more and more scenes showing Nodoka’s softer, “human” side: the girl’s sudden obsession with hugs, for example, or her experiencing a full-on mental breakdown due to hearing a simple “I love you” from her own mother – proving that, yes, underneath it all Nodoka *is* just another teenager, fundamentally not any different from all of the others.

Meanwhile, Otoha was initially portrayed as the most “normal one” in their entire class: someone without any traumas or mental issues; just your average well-off high school kid whose main and only problems in life are their grades and strict/ controlling (but ultimately still loving) parents – yet it is *Otoha* of all people who, unexpectedly, ends up sharing the most similarities with Akira himself: from her obvious wizard inclinations to the girl’s open admittance and acceptance of being a bad person.

Thus, all of their character development that happens throughout the narrative follows two similar, but inverted trajectories, like Yin and Yang: one slowly breaks away from the idea of normalcy, the other slowly rediscovers it. Otoha’s relationship with Sensei goes from “this guy is kind of a creep, but I guess I’ll tolerate his antics for now, since everyone else seems to like him fine” to “you are like a brother to me, and the only one who can truly understand me” – making it so that, ironically, it is *Otoha*, not Rin, who is Akira’s *actual* best homie at the current point in the story (cause the latter has completely neglected her homie duties, being too busy yearning for that dick) – whereas Nodoka gets severely nerfed, losing the title of “borderline undecipherable psychopath” and revealing herself to be just another morally gray tragic hero (kinda) with severe mommy issues.

Touka and Yasu, despite being probably the most dissimilar Dorm pair on a pure surface level, are nonetheless bound by their common theme of “agency” (or lack thereof) and, more specifically, “willingly following along a path laid out by a higher power”, with the same fundamental idea that there are some things in life that possess greater value than just personal independence lying at the very core of their characters. Yasu explores this subject more broadly, through a philosophical/religious lens (which makes sense in her case), while for Touka this question carries a much more practical tone, being centered around filial obligations and what it means to be a successor to something truly monumental. Regardless, both girls have a very complicated relationship with the idea of free will, neither being a stranger to occasionally questioning their “higher powers” and sometimes wondering what path they could have walked if things turned out differently, but never to the point of any true regret or disobedience: for Touka and Yasu, their role/duty always comes first, because unlike all of the other eighteen students of Class 1-A, who are individuals first and foremost, these two have been inherently *defined by* these roles for their entire life.

And that’s to say nothing of how they both were not the children their parents wanted (Touka’s father wished for a son, Yasu’s mother wished for a “normal” daughter) or the similar ostracization both girls ended up enduring before joining Sensei’s class, having no friends and no one who could truly share their beliefs/interests, despite the fact that in every other aspect their circumstances couldn’t be any more different: Touka was beloved and respected by everyone around her, having been born into a life of plenty, while Yasu was hated and feared by her family, having been completely abandoned by them and having nothing but her faith and the voices inside her head to keep her company. And, as a final similarity, they’re both initially acting as “gatekeepers” for places of meta-relevance: the Tsukioka Manor and the Cathedral – only letting inside those whom they deem “worthy”.

And, finally, we have Noriko and Kirin: two girls who are *also* Yin-Yang mirrors of each other, just like Nodoka/Otoha.

For one, both roommates initially embody the opposing extremes on each of the “selflessness/selfishness” and “sentimentality/indifference” personality spectrums, before slowly beginning to switch over to the other side: Noriko eventually gets tired of constantly being the martyr and decides to finally take something for herself for once (which also manifests as her becoming much more willing to let her actions negatively affect others, directly or indirectly, as long as Noriko herself ends up being happy – something that is clearly seen during that whole Niki debacle in 0.50), while Kirin realizes that her “I’m not like the other girls” act was actually fake as fuck and that she *is*, in fact, just like those “other girls” who want “stupid” things like love, feeling valued by your partner and proper courtship. And secondly, they both have a severe inferiority complex due to constantly living in the shadow of their more talented/successful older sister, though the ways the girls deal with these feelings of inadequacy are likewise diametrically opposed: Noriko internalizes them and tries to win over Niki by changing herself, whereas Kirin usually takes out her frustrations directly on Karin.

– Every single mother/daughter and sister/sister pair in the game (although these particular pairings are usually very unambiguously explored within the events related to the relevant characters, so I don’t think I really need to add anything here).

– Sara/Haruka/Maki trio has two main “Venn diagram intersections”: how all of them change as people under stress due to unexpected life curveballs, as well as their personal views on adult/teenager relationships. In both cases, all three women react in the exact same way, specific to their character: Maki embodies “betterment” and always tries to do what is moral/right, Haruka embodies “downfall” and always doubles down on her worst qualities, and Sara embodies “indecision” and is always stuck between the two, unable to fully commit to either light or darkness.

– Chinami and Tsukasa: both are extremely gifted children with a severe lack of personal freedom who are ready and willing to do what is expected of them (act like an innocent child in case of Chinami and “be a failsafe” in case of Tsukasa) for the sake of their families, even if it means sacrificing their own happiness in the process.

– Maya and Noriko have *a lot* of “cat vs dog” symbolism going on between them: from their visual designs (the collars they wear, for example) to their personalities (loner vs social, sly vs direct, possessive vs loyal, deeply individualistic vs eager to “be trained”) – not to mention the fact that both girls have been directly compared to their respective animal at least once in the game thus far.

– The soccer club girls: aside from Kirin/Karin pairing, which falls under the aforementioned “sisters” category, how Miku/Kirin and Miku/Karin all relate to each other is directly brought up in many of the Kanda sisters’ events in Chapter 2.

– Ayane and Kirin (their similarities and differences are openly discussed in Kirin’s “Made Out of Nothing”).

– Wakana and Osako: the commonality of “appearances can be deceiving” (Wakana is nowhere near as dead inside as she constantly pretends to be, and Osako is nowhere near as confident and self-assured as she looks while teaching karate) and the underlying theme of what it means to be in an adult romantic relationship, with all of its pitfalls, struggles and insecurities: sexual compatibility, personal boundaries, finding a healthy amount of selflessness vs selfishness, avoiding codependency, having children and so on.

– Tsubasa and Yuki (there is *at least* a shared motif of “personal freedom” and how neither is particularly happy despite being on the opposite extremes of that spectrum, but I am unsure whether there is a deeper layer to their relationship since we’ve basically just learned about it a few updates ago).

– Kaori and Nao-chan: both are “aliens” who slowly learn how to be human through mutual support, taking care of someone “weaker” than them and regularly interacting with other people. Plus, there is also is also the second overlapping trait in how Kaori’s and Nao-chan’s bodies are not *entirely* their own: the former has Sekai’s heart inside of her, while the latter intentionally looks like an amalgamation of a bunch of different characters (Ami’s and Maya’s eyes, Tsuneyo’s skin color, etcetera) – in addition to their unique speech quirks and a shared visual detail of heterochromia.

All of the other pairs are either extremely fucking obvious (like Ayane/Touka “rich girl” comparisons) or their commonalities are too vague/uninteresting for me to bother properly writing them out, since I’ve already spent *way* too much on this part alone.

Meanwhile, Otoha was initially portrayed as the most “normal one” in their entire class: someone without any traumas or mental issues; just your average well-off high school kid whose main and only problems in life are their grades and strict/ controlling (but ultimately still loving) parents – yet it is *Otoha* of all people who, unexpectedly, ends up sharing the most similarities with Akira himself: from her obvious wizard inclinations to the girl’s open admittance and acceptance of being a bad person.
Thus, all of their character development that happens throughout the narrative follows two similar, but inverted trajectories, like Yin and Yang: one slowly breaks away from the idea of normalcy, the other slowly rediscovers it. Otoha’s relationship with Sensei goes from “this guy is kind of a creep, but I guess I’ll tolerate his antics for now, since everyone else seems to like him fine” to “you are like a brother to me, and the only one who can truly understand me” – making it so that, ironically, it is *Otoha*, not Rin, who is Akira’s *actual* best homie at the current point in the story (cause the latter has completely neglected her homie duties, being too busy yearning for that dick) – whereas Nodoka gets severely nerfed, losing the title of “borderline undecipherable psychopath” and revealing herself to be just another morally gray tragic hero (kinda) with severe mommy issues.
Spoiler:
Touka and Yasu
Touka and Yasu, despite being probably the most dissimilar Dorm pair on a pure surface level, are nonetheless bound by their common theme of “agency” (or lack thereof) and, more specifically, “willingly following along a path laid out by a higher power”, with the same fundamental idea that there are some things in life that possess greater value than just personal independence lying at the very core of their characters. Yasu explores this subject more broadly, through a philosophical/religious lens (which makes sense in her case), while for Touka this question carries a much more practical tone, being centered around filial obligations and what it means to be a successor to something truly monumental. Regardless, both girls have a very complicated relationship with the idea of free will, neither being a stranger to occasionally questioning their “higher powers” and sometimes wondering what path they could have walked if things turned out differently, but never to the point of any true regret or disobedience: for Touka and Yasu, their role/duty always comes first, because unlike all of the other eighteen students of Class 1-A, who are individuals first and foremost, these two have been inherently *defined by* these roles for their entire life.
And that’s to say nothing of how they both were not the children their parents wanted (Touka’s father wished for a son, Yasu’s mother wished for a “normal” daughter) or the similar ostracization both girls ended up enduring before joining Sensei’s class, having no friends and no one who could truly share their beliefs/interests, despite the fact that in every other aspect their circumstances couldn’t be any more different: Touka was beloved and respected by everyone around her, having been born into a life of plenty, while Yasu was hated and feared by her family, having been completely abandoned by them and having nothing but her faith and the voices inside her head to keep her company. And, as a final similarity, they’re both initially acting as “gatekeepers” for places of meta-relevance: the Tsukioka Manor and the Cathedral – only letting inside those whom they deem “worthy”.
Spoiler:
Noriko and Kirin
And, finally, we have Noriko and Kirin: two girls who are *also* Yin-Yang mirrors of each other, just like Nodoka/Otoha.
For one, both roommates initially embody the opposing extremes on each of the “selflessness/selfishness” and “sentimentality/indifference” personality spectrums, before slowly beginning to switch over to the other side: Noriko eventually gets tired of constantly being the martyr and decides to finally take something for herself for once (which also manifests as her becoming much more willing to let her actions negatively affect others, directly or indirectly, as long as Noriko herself ends up being happy – something that is clearly seen during that whole Niki debacle in 0.50), while Kirin realizes that her “I’m not like the other girls” act was actually fake as fuck and that she *is*, in fact, just like those “other girls” who want “stupid” things like love, feeling valued by your partner and proper courtship. And secondly, they both have a severe inferiority complex due to constantly living in the shadow of their more talented/successful older sister, though the ways the girls deal with these feelings of inadequacy are likewise diametrically opposed: Noriko internalizes them and tries to win over Niki by changing herself, whereas Kirin usually takes out her frustrations directly on Karin.
Spoiler:
Honorable mentions
– Every single mother/daughter and sister/sister pair in the game (although these particular pairings are usually very unambiguously explored within the events related to the relevant characters, so I don’t think I really need to add anything here).
– Sara/Haruka/Maki trio has two main “Venn diagram intersections”: how all of them change as people under stress due to unexpected life curveballs, as well as their personal views on adult/teenager relationships. In both cases, all three women react in the exact same way, specific to their character: Maki embodies “betterment” and always tries to do what is moral/right, Haruka embodies “downfall” and always doubles down on her worst qualities, and Sara embodies “indecision” and is always stuck between the two, unable to fully commit to either light or darkness.
– Chinami and Tsukasa: both are extremely gifted children with a severe lack of personal freedom who are ready and willing to do what is expected of them (act like an innocent child in case of Chinami and “be a failsafe” in case of Tsukasa) for the sake of their families, even if it means sacrificing their own happiness in the process.
– Maya and Noriko have *a lot* of “cat vs dog” symbolism going on between them: from their visual designs (the collars they wear, for example) to their personalities (loner vs social, sly vs direct, possessive vs loyal, deeply individualistic vs eager to “be trained”) – not to mention the fact that both girls have been directly compared to their respective animal at least once in the game thus far.
– The soccer club girls: aside from Kirin/Karin pairing, which falls under the aforementioned “sisters” category, how Miku/Kirin and Miku/Karin all relate to each other is directly brought up in many of the Kanda sisters’ events in Chapter 2.
– Ayane and Kirin (their similarities and differences are openly discussed in Kirin’s “Made Out of Nothing”).
– Wakana and Osako: the commonality of “appearances can be deceiving” (Wakana is nowhere near as dead inside as she constantly pretends to be, and Osako is nowhere near as confident and self-assured as she looks while teaching karate) and the underlying theme of what it means to be in an adult romantic relationship, with all of its pitfalls, struggles and insecurities: sexual compatibility, personal boundaries, finding a healthy amount of selflessness vs selfishness, avoiding codependency, having children and so on.
– Tsubasa and Yuki (there is *at least* a shared motif of “personal freedom” and how neither is particularly happy despite being on the opposite extremes of that spectrum, but I am unsure whether there is a deeper layer to their relationship since we’ve basically just learned about it a few updates ago).
– Kaori and Nao-chan: both are “aliens” who slowly learn how to be human through mutual support, taking care of someone “weaker” than them and regularly interacting with other people. Plus, there is also is also the second overlapping trait in how Kaori’s and Nao-chan’s bodies are not *entirely* their own: the former has Sekai’s heart inside of her, while the latter intentionally looks like an amalgamation of a bunch of different characters (Ami’s and Maya’s eyes, Tsuneyo’s skin color, etcetera) – in addition to their unique speech quirks and a shared visual detail of heterochromia.
All of the other pairs are either extremely fucking obvious (like Ayane/Touka “rich girl” comparisons) or their commonalities are too vague/uninteresting for me to bother properly writing them out, since I’ve already spent *way* too much on this part alone.

spoilers.title: Chika and Yumi
spoilers.html: Chika and Yumi form what I call one of the three “mask pairs” among the twenty main girls, because – you guessed it – all six of those characters are defined by their apparent image not matching with who they truly are inside, though the reason for that disconnect is different between each pair. In Chika’s and Yumi’s case, it all goes back to my aforementioned point about stereotypes, because both of them wear masks that were put on them by *others*, and are simply so used to being “judged by their cover” that they don’t even bother trying to correct those constantly arising misunderstandings, unless they are made by someone close to their personal circle: people who Chika and Yumi strongly *want to* be understood by. The common theme here is both girls being defined through their surface-level appearances and relationships with their peers, except that one of them is extremely social, thriving on constant public validation, while the other is extremely anti-social and couldn’t care less what the outside world (with a few select exceptions) thinks of her – same core foundation, diametrically opposite approach.

spoilers.title: Ayane and Sana
spoilers.html:
Ayane and Sana are the second “mask pair”, though unlike the previous girls these two wear their masks completely of their own volition, as a way to deal with personal issues.

Ayane is a “fake it till you make it” kind of gal who desperately wishes to become this “perfect wife/mother” figure, but the truth of it all is that underneath the mature front Ayane constantly puts up she is *still* just a frightened teenager who is not yet capable of bearing such a burden, neither physically nor mentally. Sana’s mask, on the other hand, is (or, well, was) more of an adaptive defense mechanism than anything else: she is a seedling of an exotic flower who grew up in a climate completely unfit for someone like her, and so she ended up appearing unassuming – not because Sana *actually is* that way, but simply due to her stunted growth: acting shy and timid helped her survive and adapt to her surroundings. And, consequently, once the conditions (artificially, thanks to HOPE) changed to instead be *conductive* to her proper development, Sana quickly blossomed and revealed her true colors: dark, disturbing and poisonous.

So both girls ultimately become closer to their “true selves” over the course of the story, just one of them does it by growing *into* her mask, while the other grows *out of* it. And, as a secondary common link, the Venn diagram for Ayane and Sana also revolves around the subject of “family”: Ayane grew up in a mostly neglectful household and has a strong yearning for a family of her own, while Sana grew up with a mother who deeply cared and sacrificed everything for her, only to repay that love and sacrifice with cruel and callous disregard.

spoilers.title: Makoto and Miku
spoilers.html:
Makoto and Miku are united by their single-minded obsession with the main (and only) thing they excel at: the thing they initially focused their entire life around, but then eventually moved away from once they lost their main motivation and/or discovered something else that brings them just as much joy. Both girls are also extremely competitive, goal-driven, used to being in leadership roles, have deep-rooted self-esteem issues (Makoto’s feelings of not being appreciated due to everything she does as a class representative and Akira’s unofficial secretary, and Miku’s complex regarding her own femininity) in addition to some traumatic childhood experience that is in some way related to their parents – experience that both girls are fundamentally defined by and desperately try to hide from others.

As for the juxtaposition, there is a surface-level contrast of “very smart vs very dumb” and “intellectual vs physical” in terms of their main specializations, plus the girls’ respective histories with the subject of sex: one literally grew up around it, the other had no idea how babies are made before Sensei “corrupted” her – though, despite these differences, Makoto and Miku both end up having very high libidos, sharing the same lack of self-control and disregard towards potential consequences whenever they get horny enough.

spoilers.title: Rin and Futaba
spoilers.html:
For Rin and Futaba, their similarity lies in the hidden darkness they both carry within themselves – darkness that only reveals itself occasionally, creating a striking contrast to the girls’ usual optimistic and kind-hearted demeanor, and also shares the same two common elements: firstly, it is always directed inward, not outward, only manifesting in self-destructive ways (like Rin’s cutting or Futaba’s bulimia) rather than hurting others; and secondly, both girls are fundamentally unable to ever actually *get rid of* that darkness (for one reason or another), and so they are instead forced to live with it and learn how to deal with that suffocating curse on a day-to-day basis, simply managing its symptoms rather than raising their hopes for a more permanent solution.

The juxtaposition here, likewise, lies in how the girls’ “episodes” cause a drastic switch in their usual personalities, making them act in similarly uncharacteristic but equally opposing ways, like a direct reversal of their regular selves: normally cheerful and energetic Rin completely shuts down and becomes entirely apathetic towards everything, while normally calm and gentle Futaba becomes a cornered animal who blindly lashes out in anger against anyone who dares to approach her.

spoilers.title: Ami and Maya
spoilers.html:
Ami and Maya are the third and final “mask pair”, completing the thematic trifecta of “man vs self” and “man vs society” with “man vs God” – or, well, “man vs (ever-repeating) world”, to be more precise (there is a “Sekai” pun to be made somewhere in there). The specifics of how the fake fronts these two put up were directly caused by the supernatural circumstances they found themselves in is something that I already talked about at length in my earlier Ami analysis, so I won’t repeat any of it here.

I will, however, mention another similarity between Room 5 girls, besides their obvious and uncontested meta-relevance: the fact that both Ami and Maya have zero qualms with effectively objectifying themselves when it comes to their relationship with Sensei. Every other character in the game wants to either be treated as an equal romantic partner by him (basically 85% of the cast) or to arrange some kind of “quid pro quo” deal with the guy that is less about feelings and more about raw mutual benefits (Sana and Haruka, mainly, plus Nodoka/Otoha, Tsubasa and a few potential others), yet *those two* have consistently went above and beyond by repeatedly basing their entire personal value on one thing and one thing only: how their existence can directly benefit Akira. Neither girl particularly minds being treated like a “tool” rather than an independent individual, as long as *he* is the one using them – though, of course, the principle of juxtaposition applies here, as well: with “caretaker” Ami being externally selfless and internally selfish, and “cumdump” Maya being externally selfish and internally selfless.

spoilers.title: Molly and Tsuneyo
spoilers.html:
Molly and Tsuneyo are both eccentric weirdoes who aren’t loners by nature (unlike Nodoka, for example), but still have great difficulty properly fitting in with their peers, causing them to mostly just seek companionship in each other. Both girls also share the same mindset of treating their inherent weirdness as something to be proud of *as well as* a severe personal flaw: being perfectly content with who they are and not desire change, while also having an objective understanding of all of the ways this “strangeness” negatively affects their daily lives, needlessly complicating things that should just be second nature and instead transforming them into difficult puzzles with no clear solutions – the main difference, of course, being that Molly *chose* to be like this, while Tsuneyo had this *chosen for her*.

Finally, another trait that the two of them have in common (besides being extremely passionate about their hobbies) is the their strong personal affinity towards one of their parents: Molly takes after her mom, Tsuneyo follows in the footsteps of her dad – both of whom passed down a lot of cultural/ideological heritage to their daughters (heritage that the girls now deeply respect and appreciate, using it as a conduit to better connect with said parent), and also have a strong association with death: the latter is already one foot in the grave, and the former took her own life.

Touka and Yasu, despite being probably the most dissimilar Dorm pair on a pure surface level, are nonetheless bound by their common theme of “agency” (or lack thereof) and, more specifically, “willingly following along a path laid out by a higher power”, with the same fundamental idea that there are some things in life that possess greater value than just personal independence lying at the very core of their characters. Yasu explores this subject more broadly, through a philosophical/religious lens (which makes sense in her case), while for Touka this question carries a much more practical tone, being centered around filial obligations and what it means to be a successor to something truly monumental. Regardless, both girls have a very complicated relationship with the idea of free will, neither being a stranger to occasionally questioning their “higher powers” and sometimes wondering what path they could have walked if things turned out differently, but never to the point of any true regret or disobedience: for Touka and Yasu, their role/duty always comes first, because unlike all of the other eighteen students of Class 1-A, who are individuals first and foremost, these two have been inherently *defined by* these roles for their entire life.
And that’s to say nothing of how they both were not the children their parents wanted (Touka’s father wished for a son, Yasu’s mother wished for a “normal” daughter) or the similar ostracization both girls ended up enduring before joining Sensei’s class, having no friends and no one who could truly share their beliefs/interests, despite the fact that in every other aspect their circumstances couldn’t be any more different: Touka was beloved and respected by everyone around her, having been born into a life of plenty, while Yasu was hated and feared by her family, having been completely abandoned by them and having nothing but her faith and the voices inside her head to keep her company. And, as a final similarity, they’re both initially acting as “gatekeepers” for places of meta-relevance: the Tsukioka Manor and the Cathedral – only letting inside those whom they deem “worthy”.

spoilers.title: Noriko and Kirin
spoilers.html:
And, finally, we have Noriko and Kirin: two girls who are *also* Yin-Yang mirrors of each other, just like Nodoka/Otoha.

For one, both roommates initially embody the opposing extremes on each of the “selflessness/selfishness” and “sentimentality/indifference” personality spectrums, before slowly beginning to switch over to the other side: Noriko eventually gets tired of constantly being the martyr and decides to finally take something for herself for once (which also manifests as her becoming much more willing to let her actions negatively affect others, directly or indirectly, as long as Noriko herself ends up being happy – something that is clearly seen during that whole Niki debacle in 0.50), while Kirin realizes that her “I’m not like the other girls” act was actually fake as fuck and that she *is*, in fact, just like those “other girls” who want “stupid” things like love, feeling valued by your partner and proper courtship. And secondly, they both have a severe inferiority complex due to constantly living in the shadow of their more talented/successful older sister, though the ways the girls deal with these feelings of inadequacy are likewise diametrically opposed: Noriko internalizes them and tries to win over Niki by changing herself, whereas Kirin usually takes out her frustrations directly on Karin.

spoilers.title: Honorable mentions
spoilers.html:
– Every single mother/daughter and sister/sister pair in the game (although these particular pairings are usually very unambiguously explored within the events related to the relevant characters, so I don’t think I really need to add anything here).

– Sara/Haruka/Maki trio has two main “Venn diagram intersections”: how all of them change as people under stress due to unexpected life curveballs, as well as their personal views on adult/teenager relationships. In both cases, all three women react in the exact same way, specific to their character: Maki embodies “betterment” and always tries to do what is moral/right, Haruka embodies “downfall” and always doubles down on her worst qualities, and Sara embodies “indecision” and is always stuck between the two, unable to fully commit to either light or darkness.

– Chinami and Tsukasa: both are extremely gifted children with a severe lack of personal freedom who are ready and willing to do what is expected of them (act like an innocent child in case of Chinami and “be a failsafe” in case of Tsukasa) for the sake of their families, even if it means sacrificing their own happiness in the process.

– Maya and Noriko have *a lot* of “cat vs dog” symbolism going on between them: from their visual designs (the collars they wear, for example) to their personalities (loner vs social, sly vs direct, possessive vs loyal, deeply individualistic vs eager to “be trained”) – not to mention the fact that both girls have been directly compared to their respective animal at least once in the game thus far.

– The soccer club girls: aside from Kirin/Karin pairing, which falls under the aforementioned “sisters” category, how Miku/Kirin and Miku/Karin all relate to each other is directly brought up in many of the Kanda sisters’ events in Chapter 2.

– Ayane and Kirin (their similarities and differences are openly discussed in Kirin’s “Made Out of Nothing”).

– Wakana and Osako: the commonality of “appearances can be deceiving” (Wakana is nowhere near as dead inside as she constantly pretends to be, and Osako is nowhere near as confident and self-assured as she looks while teaching karate) and the underlying theme of what it means to be in an adult romantic relationship, with all of its pitfalls, struggles and insecurities: sexual compatibility, personal boundaries, finding a healthy amount of selflessness vs selfishness, avoiding codependency, having children and so on.

– Tsubasa and Yuki (there is *at least* a shared motif of “personal freedom” and how neither is particularly happy despite being on the opposite extremes of that spectrum, but I am unsure whether there is a deeper layer to their relationship since we’ve basically just learned about it a few updates ago).

– Kaori and Nao-chan: both are “aliens” who slowly learn how to be human through mutual support, taking care of someone “weaker” than them and regularly interacting with other people. Plus, there is also is also the second overlapping trait in how Kaori’s and Nao-chan’s bodies are not *entirely* their own: the former has Sekai’s heart inside of her, while the latter intentionally looks like an amalgamation of a bunch of different characters (Ami’s and Maya’s eyes, Tsuneyo’s skin color, etcetera) – in addition to their unique speech quirks and a shared visual detail of heterochromia.

We can say Niki had it coming all that we want, but if that was enough, there'd be no one willing to give a chance to broken people anymore. Being happy isn't her actual priority, she wants to rehabilitate Akira, a lot of it coming from guilt from having stopped her parents from saving Akira from Sekai.

Noriko has been playing second fiddle to her sister her entire life. It's not like she came in like a homewrecker to a perfect relationship. She has "let" Niki go and have her second shot with Akira, even though she could have just not helped her by giving Akira the letters. So she's seeing Akira fuck pretty much everyone but her, and Niki playing pretend like she doesn't see it, and how is this changing anything really? She knows Niki's just going to blame Akira for it pretty much and that she won't actually lose her sister over it. Kind of unfair, from her perspective, that literally everyone gets to fuck Akira and Niki just pretends not to see it, with her being the sole exception.

And Akira, well, let's be real here. For all his justification of "I want to actually save Niki from myself since she's unwilling to", I do think he actually believes that, because it's the second time he's done it. I just don't think any justification is even needed at this point. So he fucked Niki's sister, so what? How does this actually change anything? It doesn't. Niki is still oathbound to help him, and he didn't intend to have a happy ending with her in the first place. Zero loss situation (other than one particular sex partner, but he has more sex partners than days in a month).
And speaking of outside the plot, I do agree that the only one that can "cheat" is the one that made a commitment in the first place. If there's a couple and a third person has sex with one of them, the cheater is the one from the couple, not the outsider. The outsider has broken no commitment - which adds to the bizarre of taking revenge on the outsider instead of blaming the actual cheater.

That being said, I think there is such a thing as betrayal in friendships, or sisterhoods. I have never dated exes from my actual friends because that was just not worth the hassle. There's enough people in the world that I don't need to invite potential damage into a precious relationship. And while dating exes desn't constitute betrayal to most friendships, they do to others. To actually do something to their current partner is just unthinkable to me. Again, by logic, the outsider isn't cheating - but it is very much a betrayal.

The difficulty here is gauging how it changes between actual siblings and just friends. To me, it will vary greatly in terms of the concept of family to each person. Sometimes a family bond is taken for granted because it's harder to break, and thus, even if you pull some fucked up shit, it will eventually settle down - whereas a friendship might just be broken forever.

Would someone in Niki's position hold Noriko in contempt forever or even "break things off" with her sibling? I really don't think she would. Even if Noriko was an adult and if Akira wasn't fucking anyone else but Niki. Noriko's been in love with him her entire life, just as Niki has. While not making it okay, it definitely does lessen the hit in the long term.
On a side-note: taking it just from a pure logical standpoint, Noriko had nothing that substancial to lose long-term in her relationship with Niki. In fact, if Akira was a smart person instead of that mess, he could probably work Niki's guilt to turn the sisters into sister-wives and have a bunch of pink-haired Himawaris (if he'd settle down with just the two of them).

To answer your specific question here you can't progress past Yumi's sixth event until you've seen Rin's ninth event ('Nothing was missing, except me'), which in itself is locked behind a certain level of progression with Ayane and both behind a certain level of progression with the main events (specifically you can't do that Rin event until you've done the main event 'Missing' and Ayane's event 'Imprinting').

The story in LiL is all tight and tied together and it's a very long game, it's not one of those harem games where you can pick your favourite girl and just do her "route" - although every character will eventually have their own monogamous purity route, though that's still years away at this point.

So yeah, like Kll said, download the guide mod for your own sake - not only will it save you a lot of time when the triggers aren't obvious or typical but if you're wanting to make only "correct" choices in order to see every event you've already locked yourself out of a couple of Rin's events down the line because you progressed Chika too fast. That's not necessarily a bad thing mind you, Sensei and Rin's dynamic changes quite a bit depending on how fast you progress Chika so it's interesting to do it this way regardless but I thought you should know lol

Tbf to him, I personally think he is actually really good at character design. I feel that almost all of the characters are designed in a way that accurately represent their personalities or at least what they are supposed to represent (see CW26's recent analysis on 'stereotype subversion' etc.) while also making them look quite unique.

That being said, I don't believe he actively produced any of the assets, i.e. clothes etc, that they wear other than I guess writing dumb shit on them ("I <3 poor people", "blue shirt" etc.) although I might be wrong on this one, feel free to correct me.
He still, at the very least, decided what they are supposed to look like, what they wear in which scenario, their facial expressions etc. so in that sense I feel like he as a much better knack for good design decisions compared to most developers, at least the ones using the Koikatsu engine.

And Sensei, although I'm sure everyone got used to it by now - he objectively looks fucking dumb. But that's more on KK and completely neglecting male character customization, I suppose.

CharlotteWiltshire26 said:
this post is a response to people who have been repeatedly criticizing many of Selebus’ decisions as a writer for the last couple of years and expressing their severe dissatisfaction with the current state of LiL - arguing that the guy is just a pretentious hack who is only decent at best and is *definitely* nowhere near as good as he pretends to be.
Click to expand...
The major criticism of chapter 4 wasn't ever that Selebus was a pretentious hack, it was that he left Akira as a passive protagonist way too long, while abandoning an increasing focus on solving the reset mysteries. He began to effectively minimize most of the supernatural presented thus far as a smokescreen (lore of the two, that were three, that were four), and shift to unlimited derivation in the form of the god of the week.

The minor criticisms weren't that he was a hack either, but that he sometimes either lost his touch on managing the tone of the collective events of a single update (like Imani's dormwars and the recent one with Nodokathon 2), or his sudden choice to introduce many instances of love interests being railed by people other than Akira, often being raped either in the past or present, when that was never a feature of the game to this extent.

Lastly, many have raised valid concerns in relation to potential inconsistencies like in "Kyoto" or regarding to "Ami's reveal". And while those aren't confirmed inconsistencies, they aren't totally debunked either - and, as many have pointed out, they are quite "convenient" if not retcons. Like the whole "Niki always knew all of a sudden".
Selebus writing is quite good at times, and at others is quite flawed. Mostly, it is decent - and that's it. For instance, from the examples you yourself evoked, you say that one of his strengths is going beyond an initial assumption of a character, like Chika being just a gyaru, or Yumi being just a bully.

But isn't that just very basic writing? If you were to write a character, unless your intention was to have a "gyaru" or a "tsundere" or a "token whatever", and have them be just that, you would think "okay, but what are they beyond it?" or "why are they like this?".

It goes back to what usually accompanies the criticism of his writing being "decent at best", which is that most of the praise for Selebus' writing comes from the fact that it is amazing writing for its genre (adult porn games). You'd hardly find anyone being surprised at reading a nicely rated novel and finding a character that has some depth beyond literal first impressions.
Here is the full list of the character's archetypes provided by you:
Chika as a “basic” and vapid gyaru;
Yumi as a callous and cruel bully;
Ayane as a clingy and obsessive “I’m in love with Sensei, and it’s my only personality trait” girl;
Sana as someone extremely shy, timid and reserved;
Makoto as a smart and diligent class president who doesn’t care about anything except studying;
Miku as a dumb hyperactive tomboy;
Rin as an outgoing and happy-go-lucky gal with no personal problems besides being aggressively bisexual;
Futaba as someone exceedingly nice and gentle, to the point of being unable to stand up for herself;
Ami as an innocent and airheaded “girly girl”;
Maya as cold and distant, and the sole bastion of “won’t be tempted to sleep with Sensei even in a million years”;
Molly as a weeb-bait white gamer girl;
Tsuneyo as a sheltered comic relief character;
Uta as a flirt with a lot of self-confidence;
Io as an asocial, asexual loner;
Nodoka as a quirky incest-obsessed genius;
Otoha as just… kind of normal;
Touka as a walking-talking rich girl cliché;
Yasu as a creepy religious nutcase;
Noriko as a yandere-esque stalker with no filter;
and Kirin as a hedonist who only cares about sex.
But then, in my opinion:
Maya and Ami are the only ones of your list that really aren't what they appear to be.

Chika is a basic gyaru that skips class to watch Niki's interviews, and dresses flashy. This is not a misdirection.
Yumi is a callous and cruel bully that goes against Futaba for no reason whatsoever, there's no deeper story there.
Ayane is clingy and obsessive to the extent of taking photos from Akira while he sleeps, hanging them over her bed and even having his phone cloned.
Sana is so shy that she develops PTSD from spaghetti.
Miku is a dumb hyperactive tomboy, despite of her PTSD.
Rin is a disaster lesbian, despite her depression.
Futaba is someone that even after all these years still can't stand up for herself.
Molly is a horny gamer girl, her mother having killed herself or not.
Tsuneyo is a sheltered girl that doesn't even know what it means to "fuck someone".
Uta and Io kind of are what they appear, there's just reasons for that.
Nodoka is so "genius" that it takes people out of the narrative.
Otoha still is kind of normal.
Touka never stopped being the rich girl.
Noriko still drugged Akira to win a competition and fucked him in front of her sister.
Kirin is still fucked up to the point of blackmailing and sexually assaulting Ayane.
Most of what we learn about the girls isn't even an unveiling of their initial impressions, they're just additional information. Thus, most of these archetypes are just "true" (to the extent that they represent a fraction of how these people behave).

But what if Chika dressed flashy because she had to go on compensated dating to support Chinami? That'd be a reversal of her not being a "gyaru" at all. What if Rin suddenly found a medication that worked and found out that being that hormonal was an imbalance rather than her true personality? Those would be actual spins on their archetypes.

But what Selebus does is just add information, or give them a reason as to why they're that way. While that's more realistic writing surely, it isn't that amazing either? (if compared to good writing overall).
I quite enjoy parts of the writing (like the intro narration) and I detest others (like many of Akira's repetitive monologues). I feel like an increasing number of people tend to pay less attention to writing outside of dialogues now too. Anyway, enjoyment has nothing to do with quality of writing either - I quite enjoy half-translated webnovels that weren't that well written in their original language to begin with.

Miku as a dumb hyperactive tomboy;

Futaba as someone exceedingly nice and gentle, to the point of being unable to stand up for herself;
Ami as an innocent and airheaded “girly girl”;
Maya as cold and distant, and the sole bastion of “won’t be tempted to sleep with Sensei even in a million years”;
Molly as a weeb-bait white gamer girl;
Tsuneyo as a sheltered comic relief character;
Uta as a flirt with a lot of self-confidence;
Io as an asocial, asexual loner;
Nodoka as a quirky incest-obsessed genius;
Otoha as just… kind of normal;
Touka as a walking-talking rich girl cliché;
Yasu as a creepy religious nutcase;
Noriko as a yandere-esque stalker with no filter;
and Kirin as a hedonist who only cares about sex.
But then, in my opinion:
Maya and Ami are the only ones of your list that really aren't what they appear to be.

Chika is a basic gyaru that skips class to watch Niki's interviews, and dresses flashy. This is not a misdirection.
Yumi is a callous and cruel bully that goes against Futaba for no reason whatsoever, there's no deeper story there.
Ayane is clingy and obsessive to the extent of taking photos from Akira while he sleeps, hanging them over her bed and even having his phone cloned.
Sana is so shy that she develops PTSD from spaghetti.
Miku is a dumb hyperactive tomboy, despite of her PTSD.
Rin is a disaster lesbian, despite her depression.
Futaba is someone that even after all these years still can't stand up for herself.

Uta and Io kind of are what they appear, there's just reasons for that.
Nodoka is so "genius" that it takes people out of the narrative.
Otoha still is kind of normal.
Touka never stopped being the rich girl.
Noriko still drugged Akira to win a competition and fucked him in front of her sister.
Kirin is still fucked up to the point of blackmailing and sexually assaulting Ayane.
Most of what we learn about the girls isn't even an unveiling of their initial impressions, they're just additional information. Thus, most of these archetypes are just "true" (to the extent that they represent a fraction of how these people behave).

What if Rin suddenly found a medication that worked and found out that being that hormonal was an imbalance rather than her true personality? Those would be actual spins on their archetypes.

But what Selebus does is just add information, or give them a reason as to why they're that way. While that's more realistic writing surely, it isn't that amazing either? (if compared to good writing overall).

I get where everyone is coming from; However, I think it's also a bit of a trap.

It feels this way mostly because we're stuck experiencing this in real time. I've only been involved since September, and hate the wait, so I can only imagine how it feels for those that have waited 5 years.

Yet, as someone that reads and writes fanfiction, serialized fiction takes time...and generally the reading enjoyment outcome is different over being presented with a final product.

Imagine, 5-6 years from now, a new reader starts LIL.

Chances are they walk away thinking it's one of, if not the best, VN ever written. The complete product, 400+ hours of content, plus all the various routes?

It would be hard to argue that it isn't, at that point.

BUT, that reader isn't waiting 10 years. They get it, and 6 months later all the answers are in their hands. Or at least their first playthrough! Lmao

Imagine how you'd feel, enjoyment wise, if the game was already done. You'd be extremely satisfied, most likely. The biggest complaints(months without content for their 'best girl', Akira taking fucking forever to get shit done, mystery bullshit, etc) would all be gone if the game was done.

In that vein, if all those complaints were taken care of simply by the game being finished....could you truly say that Selebus isn't at bare minimum....a great writer?

It's a hypothetical, sure. But I imagine I'd feel that way, once the rollercoaster is over. My complaints would be, while justified now during the wait, likely all buttoned down.

The major criticism of chapter 4 wasn't ever that Selebus was a pretentious hack, it was that he left Akira as a passive protagonist way too long, while abandoning an increasing focus on solving the reset mysteries. He began to effectively minimize most of the supernatural presented thus far as a smokescreen (lore of the two, that were three, that were four), and shift to unlimited derivation in the form of the god of the week.

Yes, I am well aware that these were all things people had issues with – it’s just that, well, I kinda fundamentally disagree with them on that front and don’t really see any of the examples you listed as *actual* flaws in the writing:

– Sensei “becoming a passive protagonist for far too long” makes perfect sense from a writing perspective, because it is entirely consistent with how his character was presented to us beforehand. We *know* that this is just how he reacts to severe emotional loss, so this development doesn’t come out of nowhere – which is exactly why I personally don’t have any issues with it. The game intentionally spends a lot of time in earlier Chapters painting a very unflattering picture of just how much of a trainwreck Akira became after Sekai’s death, and the beginning of Chapter 4 is a direct repeat of that situation – with all that entails – allowing us to witness his mental breakdown firsthand. Now, was it “fun” or “engaging” to watch the guy endlessly mop around or constantly spout depressive and self-deprecating monologues? Perhaps not to everybody. But it *did* allow the narrative to focus on characters *other* than Sensei, to show us how their lives change and develop *beyond* the scope of just their one-on-one interactions with Akira, without his shadow perpetually looming over them – which was, IMO, a fully welcome and beneficial change that only made the story better, not worse. Plus, I hate whenever characters in fiction get back to normal *way* too quickly afer experiencing what is effectively a life-shattering event, so Sensei battling his depression and apathy for the entire Chapter thus far felt both organic and realistic.

– “Abandoning an increasing focus on solving the Reset mysteries” is also a flaw *only* if you approach Lessons in Love from a fairly narrow-minded perspective of “this is explicitly a story about how the characters are trying to find a way to escape the never-ending time loop, and everything else that happens is entirely secondary to that main overarching goal”, which just isn’t true. The Resets are nothing more than a set dressing, a convenient narrative device to facilitate what LiL *actually* is about: exploration of trauma, forbidden relationships, family, personal growth/regression and many other things – in the similar vein of how Umineko isn’t *actually* about “solving the murders” or Homestuck isn’t *actually* about “playing Sburb”. These are all grand, multi-faceted narratives that use relatively simple and easily-understood plot hooks as a simple backdrop to keep you entertained during the earlier parts, until the full brunt of their thematic complexity finally sets in. Besides, the beginning of Chapter 4 was, like, barely 40% into the entirety of LiL, and we’re still just recently passed the approximate halfway point – focusing *too much* on grand narrative revelations regarding Resets at this point in time would have been very premature on Selebus’ part.

– “Shift to unlimited derivation in the form of the god of the week” *could* be pretty jarring/annoying for some people, I’ll admit, but as long as these “Gods of the week” mostly stay in the background in the form of occasional references and one-off appearances rather than become the sole focus of the paranormal side of narrative – which *is* the case as of right now, because Pareidolia, Ami, Nodoka, Sekaori and Nao-chan all individually played a much bigger role in Chapter 4 in terms of the meta-stuff than *all* of the “new Gods” combined – I still maintain that all of this remains in the realm of “subjective preferences” rather than “objective narrative flaw”. Personally, I played Disco Elysium, both Pathologic games and read most of Haruki Murakami’s works – some strange surreal shit just casually happening in the story with zero buildup or fanfare for the sake of “vibes” rather than direct story significance doesn’t faze me in the slightest.

– Full disclosure: I am one of the few rare LiL fans who genuinely enjoys Dorm Wars, so I never really had any issues with the seeming tone dissonance of some of the latest DW installments a lot of people apparently complained about, because it all goes back to my earlier-made point about intentional juxtaposition. The “Sports War” served as a well-needed breath of levity after the depression marathon that was the entire beginning of Chapter 4 (in addition to clearly showcasing how their collective Akira withdrawal slowly causes all of Class 1-A to progressively get more and more unhinged as the days go by), and both Nodokathons always made perfect sense to me in terms of their placement within the narrative: all of the participants had plausible reasons for both being selected by Nodoka and actually choosing to attend, their borderline out-of-character horny behavior could be easily explained by them being permanently hormonal teenagers in the throes of their puberty (I myself once went to a similar “group event” when I was their age, so I have a first-hand experience with how that secretive, intimate atmosphere can easily erode your inhibitions), and Nodoka’s own motives in regards to what she hoped to achieve by organizing Nodokathons have been pretty much openly stated both times, so this wasn’t a random or out-of-character thing for her either.

– NTR shit is stupid, and that’s really all there is to say on the matter.

– As for the inconsistencies… well, it’s hard to say for sure – perhaps you are right. I never implied that Selebus is *infallible*, however – only that he is really, really good at what he does. The dude obviously isn’t perfect – no one is – and when you’re writing a story of LiL’s complexity while *also* being on a severe deadline, some unfortunate mistakes are bound to come up here and there, regardless of how much you try to prevent them – that’s just how it works. I’m not excusing these “retcons” (if that’s what they are, of course), but rather pointing out that – in my opinion, anyway – they are relatively small flaws in an otherwise almost flawless narrative, and that, when judged as a writer, Selebus deserves a lot more praise for his successes than condemnation of his failures. You disagreeing with me on Lessons in Love being anywhere near “flawless” is fine – I wholeheartedly respect your opinion – but that’s just how I see it, plain and simple.

The specific strength of Selebus’ writing that I was trying to convey in the “Stereotype Subversion” part of my analysis isn’t just “going beyond an initial assumption of a character” – it’s “going beyond an initial assumption of a character in a way that *directly subverts* your original perspective on them *without* it feeling forced or completely out of left field”.

It’s one thing to simply learn a new piece of information that makes all of the seemingly irrelevant details neatly fall into place and finally reveal the full picture – and quite another to suddenly come to a realization that the puzzle you’ve been trying to assemble all this time doesn’t actually exist, and that its pieces, when properly put together, reveal something else entirely. The former *is* just basic good writing, yes, but the latter is not, because it takes much more careful planning and extra care in order to create both an effective/believable “fake front” *and* and an equally fitting/satisfying “truth” that don’t contradict each other in any way, shape or form – without creating a “Logic Error”, in Umineko terms.

Almost all of the counterexamples you bring up about the characters “being who they initially appear to be” are from Chapter 1 or early Chapter 2 – as in, still effectively the beginning part of the story where their “stereotypes” are either still being established or haven’t been fully subverted yet. Can you do the same for the later parts of LiL, though? How many instances are there of Chika still acting like a superficial “basic gyaru”, or Yumi bullying people, or Sana being extremely timid and reserved, or Tsuneyo not properly understanding the implications of what is happening, or Touka behaving like a stereotypical “rich girl” (as well as any other relevant stereotypical traits for the rest of the cast) throughout the second half of Chapter 3 and the entirety of Chapter 4? Maybe you could cherry-pick a few among some of the more light-hearted and comedic scenes, sure, but during the truly serious stuff? Suddenly Makoto no longer cares about following rules or studying, Miku shows actual insight and proactive thinking (like during Maki’s recent 0.55 events), Yasu is sweet and vulnerable rather than creepy and annoying, Otoha is not even remotely “normal”, Kirin’s reaction to Haruka’s advances in 0.54 is a drastic departure from her “unwanted sexual contact – what is that, lol?” line she drops during “Dyed Orange, Drenched in Sun” – etcetera. These are *not* the same archetypical, clearly defined characters that were presented to us during their first five-ten personal events, and the difference here is much greater than the simple “well, I know their trauma now, so that explains everything” – or at least that’s how my schizo brain interprets it.

Finally, you say “most of the praise for Selebus' writing comes from the fact that it is amazing writing for its genre (adult porn games) – you'd hardly find anyone being surprised at reading a nicely rated novel and finding a character that has some depth beyond literal first impressions” – but that’s, sadly, not really the case (not in my experience, anyway).

To be fully transparent, I have zero intention of turning this into a dick-measuring contest and resorting to arguments such as “well, I read/watched/played [X], [Y] and [Z], while you didn’t, so I am automatically more qualified to make objective statements about the quality of fiction than you are”, but I can genuinely count the number of stories I know that could *even remotely* contest with Lessons in Love in terms of the quality of their writing on one hand. Most of the fiction I normally engage with falls somewhere on the spectrum between “good”, “great” or even “outstanding” – and, obviously, there is an equal number of unfortunate examples that belong to the categories of “abysmal”, “bad” or “mediocre” – yet in terms of being directly comparable to LiL, of all things, there are *none*. Now, I fully admit that this evaluation is at least partially dictated by my own personal biases, sure, but even outside of those there is just *way too much* excellence in Selebus’ creation, way too many clever connections, and thematic depth, and clearly visible effort for it all to just be a product of my imagination – and so I will continue to relentlessly argue in LiL’s favor whenever I can, out of pure and selfless love for what I consider to be the work of true art.

Likewise, I strongly resent the implication that the genre of “adult porn games” is somehow inherently different from any other genre of fiction, to the point where it has to be judged on its own separate metrics rather than the same scale we use for everything else. I view Lessons in Love through the same critical lens I view Hermann Hesse’s “Demian”, or Breaking Bad, or Umineko, or any of the games made by Ice-Pick Lodge and Project Moon – and it doesn’t matter that LiL is technically “porn” while all of the other examples I listed aren’t, because my ability/inability to masturbate to a piece of fiction does not affect how I approach it: neither emotionally nor intellectually.

And while I do fundamentally agree with your statement that “enjoyment has nothing to do with quality of writing” – because, yes, subjectivity will *always* trump objectivity in this particular case – as someone who is *extremely* anal about the quality of prose in my text-based media, unimaginative, redundant or badly translated text just immediately takes me out of it.

Now, I fully admit that this evaluation is at least partially dictated by my own personal biases, sure, but even outside of those there is just *way too much* excellence in Selebus’ creation, way too many clever connections, and thematic depth, and clearly visible effort for it all to just be a product of my imagination – and so I will continue to relentlessly argue in LiL’s favor whenever I can, out of pure and selfless love for what I consider to be the work of true art.
Likewise, I strongly resent the implication that the genre of “adult porn games” is somehow inherently different from any other genre of fiction, to the point where it has to be judged on its own separate metrics rather than the same scale we use for everything else. I view Lessons in Love through the same critical lens I view Hermann Hesse’s “Demian”, or Breaking Bad, or Umineko, or any of the games made by Ice-Pick Lodge and Project Moon – and it doesn’t matter that LiL is technically “porn” while all of the other examples I listed aren’t, because my ability/inability to masturbate to a piece of fiction does not affect how I approach it: neither emotionally nor intellectually.
And while I do fundamentally agree with your statement that “enjoyment has nothing to do with quality of writing” – because, yes, subjectivity will *always* trump objectivity in this particular case – as someone who is *extremely* anal about the quality of prose in my text-based media, unimaginative, redundant or badly translated text just immediately takes me out of it.

spoilers.title: Selebus criticisms
spoilers.html:
The major criticism of chapter 4 wasn't ever that Selebus was a pretentious hack, it was that he left Akira as a passive protagonist way too long, while abandoning an increasing focus on solving the reset mysteries. He began to effectively minimize most of the supernatural presented thus far as a smokescreen (lore of the two, that were three, that were four), and shift to unlimited derivation in the form of the god of the week.

The minor criticisms weren't that he was a hack either, but that he sometimes either lost his touch on managing the tone of the collective events of a single update (like Imani's dormwars and the recent one with Nodokathon 2), or his sudden choice to introduce many instances of love interests being railed by people other than Akira, often being raped either in the past or present, when that was never a feature of the game to this extent.

Lastly, many have raised valid concerns in relation to potential inconsistencies like in "Kyoto" or regarding to "Ami's reveal". And while those aren't confirmed inconsistencies, they aren't totally debunked either - and, as many have pointed out, they are quite "convenient" if not retcons. Like the whole "Niki always knew all of a sudden".

spoilers.title: more detailed analysis
spoilers.html:
Here is the full list of the character's archetypes provided by you:
Chika as a “basic” and vapid gyaru;
Yumi as a callous and cruel bully;
Ayane as a clingy and obsessive “I’m in love with Sensei, and it’s my only personality trait” girl;
Sana as someone extremely shy, timid and reserved;
Makoto as a smart and diligent class president who doesn’t care about anything except studying;
Miku as a dumb hyperactive tomboy;
Rin as an outgoing and happy-go-lucky gal with no personal problems besides being aggressively bisexual;
Futaba as someone exceedingly nice and gentle, to the point of being unable to stand up for herself;
Ami as an innocent and airheaded “girly girl”;
Maya as cold and distant, and the sole bastion of “won’t be tempted to sleep with Sensei even in a million years”;
Molly as a weeb-bait white gamer girl;
Tsuneyo as a sheltered comic relief character;
Uta as a flirt with a lot of self-confidence;
Io as an asocial, asexual loner;
Nodoka as a quirky incest-obsessed genius;
Otoha as just… kind of normal;
Touka as a walking-talking rich girl cliché;
Yasu as a creepy religious nutcase;
Noriko as a yandere-esque stalker with no filter;
and Kirin as a hedonist who only cares about sex.
But then, in my opinion:
Maya and Ami are the only ones of your list that really aren't what they appear to be.

Chika is a basic gyaru that skips class to watch Niki's interviews, and dresses flashy. This is not a misdirection.
Yumi is a callous and cruel bully that goes against Futaba for no reason whatsoever, there's no deeper story there.
Ayane is clingy and obsessive to the extent of taking photos from Akira while he sleeps, hanging them over her bed and even having his phone cloned.
Sana is so shy that she develops PTSD from spaghetti.
Miku is a dumb hyperactive tomboy, despite of her PTSD.
Rin is a disaster lesbian, despite her depression.
Futaba is someone that even after all these years still can't stand up for herself.
Molly is a horny gamer girl, her mother having killed herself or not.
Tsuneyo is a sheltered girl that doesn't even know what it means to "fuck someone".
Uta and Io kind of are what they appear, there's just reasons for that.
Nodoka is so "genius" that it takes people out of the narrative.
Otoha still is kind of normal.
Touka never stopped being the rich girl.
Noriko still drugged Akira to win a competition and fucked him in front of her sister.
Kirin is still fucked up to the point of blackmailing and sexually assaulting Ayane.
Most of what we learn about the girls isn't even an unveiling of their initial impressions, they're just additional information. Thus, most of these archetypes are just "true" (to the extent that they represent a fraction of how these people behave).

But what if Chika dressed flashy because she had to go on compensated dating to support Chinami? That'd be a reversal of her not being a "gyaru" at all. What if Rin suddenly found a medication that worked and found out that being that hormonal was an imbalance rather than her true personality? Those would be actual spins on their archetypes.

But what Selebus does is just add information, or give them a reason as to why they're that way. While that's more realistic writing surely, it isn't that amazing either? (if compared to good writing overall).
