spoilers.title: Selebus criticisms
spoilers.html:
Yes, I am well aware that these were all things people had issues with – it’s just that, well, I kinda fundamentally disagree with them on that front and don’t really see any of the examples you listed as *actual* flaws in the writing:

– Sensei “becoming a passive protagonist for far too long” makes perfect sense from a writing perspective, because it is entirely consistent with how his character was presented to us beforehand. We *know* that this is just how he reacts to severe emotional loss, so this development doesn’t come out of nowhere – which is exactly why I personally don’t have any issues with it. The game intentionally spends a lot of time in earlier Chapters painting a very unflattering picture of just how much of a trainwreck Akira became after Sekai’s death, and the beginning of Chapter 4 is a direct repeat of that situation – with all that entails – allowing us to witness his mental breakdown firsthand. Now, was it “fun” or “engaging” to watch the guy endlessly mop around or constantly spout depressive and self-deprecating monologues? Perhaps not to everybody. But it *did* allow the narrative to focus on characters *other* than Sensei, to show us how their lives change and develop *beyond* the scope of just their one-on-one interactions with Akira, without his shadow perpetually looming over them – which was, IMO, a fully welcome and beneficial change that only made the story better, not worse. Plus, I hate whenever characters in fiction get back to normal *way* too quickly afer experiencing what is effectively a life-shattering event, so Sensei battling his depression and apathy for the entire Chapter thus far felt both organic and realistic.

– “Abandoning an increasing focus on solving the Reset mysteries” is also a flaw *only* if you approach Lessons in Love from a fairly narrow-minded perspective of “this is explicitly a story about how the characters are trying to find a way to escape the never-ending time loop, and everything else that happens is entirely secondary to that main overarching goal”, which just isn’t true. The Resets are nothing more than a set dressing, a convenient narrative device to facilitate what LiL *actually* is about: exploration of trauma, forbidden relationships, family, personal growth/regression and many other things – in the similar vein of how Umineko isn’t *actually* about “solving the murders” or Homestuck isn’t *actually* about “playing Sburb”. These are all grand, multi-faceted narratives that use relatively simple and easily-understood plot hooks as a simple backdrop to keep you entertained during the earlier parts, until the full brunt of their thematic complexity finally sets in. Besides, the beginning of Chapter 4 was, like, barely 40% into the entirety of LiL, and we’re still just recently passed the approximate halfway point – focusing *too much* on grand narrative revelations regarding Resets at this point in time would have been very premature on Selebus’ part.

– “Shift to unlimited derivation in the form of the god of the week” *could* be pretty jarring/annoying for some people, I’ll admit, but as long as these “Gods of the week” mostly stay in the background in the form of occasional references and one-off appearances rather than become the sole focus of the paranormal side of narrative – which *is* the case as of right now, because Pareidolia, Ami, Nodoka, Sekaori and Nao-chan all individually played a much bigger role in Chapter 4 in terms of the meta-stuff than *all* of the “new Gods” combined – I still maintain that all of this remains in the realm of “subjective preferences” rather than “objective narrative flaw”. Personally, I played Disco Elysium, both Pathologic games and read most of Haruki Murakami’s works – some strange surreal shit just casually happening in the story with zero buildup or fanfare for the sake of “vibes” rather than direct story significance doesn’t faze me in the slightest.

– Full disclosure: I am one of the few rare LiL fans who genuinely enjoys Dorm Wars, so I never really had any issues with the seeming tone dissonance of some of the latest DW installments a lot of people apparently complained about, because it all goes back to my earlier-made point about intentional juxtaposition. The “Sports War” served as a well-needed breath of levity after the depression marathon that was the entire beginning of Chapter 4 (in addition to clearly showcasing how their collective Akira withdrawal slowly causes all of Class 1-A to progressively get more and more unhinged as the days go by), and both Nodokathons always made perfect sense to me in terms of their placement within the narrative: all of the participants had plausible reasons for both being selected by Nodoka and actually choosing to attend, their borderline out-of-character horny behavior could be easily explained by them being permanently hormonal teenagers in the throes of their puberty (I myself once went to a similar “group event” when I was their age, so I have a first-hand experience with how that secretive, intimate atmosphere can easily erode your inhibitions), and Nodoka’s own motives in regards to what she hoped to achieve by organizing Nodokathons have been pretty much openly stated both times, so this wasn’t a random or out-of-character thing for her either.

– NTR shit is stupid, and that’s really all there is to say on the matter.

– As for the inconsistencies… well, it’s hard to say for sure – perhaps you are right. I never implied that Selebus is *infallible*, however – only that he is really, really good at what he does. The dude obviously isn’t perfect – no one is – and when you’re writing a story of LiL’s complexity while *also* being on a severe deadline, some unfortunate mistakes are bound to come up here and there, regardless of how much you try to prevent them – that’s just how it works. I’m not excusing these “retcons” (if that’s what they are, of course), but rather pointing out that – in my opinion, anyway – they are relatively small flaws in an otherwise almost flawless narrative, and that, when judged as a writer, Selebus deserves a lot more praise for his successes than condemnation of his failures. You disagreeing with me on Lessons in Love being anywhere near “flawless” is fine – I wholeheartedly respect your opinion – but that’s just how I see it, plain and simple.

spoilers.title: Further clarifications about my earlier post
spoilers.html:
The specific strength of Selebus’ writing that I was trying to convey in the “Stereotype Subversion” part of my analysis isn’t just “going beyond an initial assumption of a character” – it’s “going beyond an initial assumption of a character in a way that *directly subverts* your original perspective on them *without* it feeling forced or completely out of left field”.

It’s one thing to simply learn a new piece of information that makes all of the seemingly irrelevant details neatly fall into place and finally reveal the full picture – and quite another to suddenly come to a realization that the puzzle you’ve been trying to assemble all this time doesn’t actually exist, and that its pieces, when properly put together, reveal something else entirely. The former *is* just basic good writing, yes, but the latter is not, because it takes much more careful planning and extra care in order to create both an effective/believable “fake front” *and* and an equally fitting/satisfying “truth” that don’t contradict each other in any way, shape or form – without creating a “Logic Error”, in Umineko terms.

Almost all of the counterexamples you bring up about the characters “being who they initially appear to be” are from Chapter 1 or early Chapter 2 – as in, still effectively the beginning part of the story where their “stereotypes” are either still being established or haven’t been fully subverted yet. Can you do the same for the later parts of LiL, though? How many instances are there of Chika still acting like a superficial “basic gyaru”, or Yumi bullying people, or Sana being extremely timid and reserved, or Tsuneyo not properly understanding the implications of what is happening, or Touka behaving like a stereotypical “rich girl” (as well as any other relevant stereotypical traits for the rest of the cast) throughout the second half of Chapter 3 and the entirety of Chapter 4? Maybe you could cherry-pick a few among some of the more light-hearted and comedic scenes, sure, but during the truly serious stuff? Suddenly Makoto no longer cares about following rules or studying, Miku shows actual insight and proactive thinking (like during Maki’s recent 0.55 events), Yasu is sweet and vulnerable rather than creepy and annoying, Otoha is not even remotely “normal”, Kirin’s reaction to Haruka’s advances in 0.54 is a drastic departure from her “unwanted sexual contact – what is that, lol?” line she drops during “Dyed Orange, Drenched in Sun” – etcetera. These are *not* the same archetypical, clearly defined characters that were presented to us during their first five-ten personal events, and the difference here is much greater than the simple “well, I know their trauma now, so that explains everything” – or at least that’s how my schizo brain interprets it.

spoilers.title: General writing discussion
spoilers.html:
Finally, you say “most of the praise for Selebus' writing comes from the fact that it is amazing writing for its genre (adult porn games) – you'd hardly find anyone being surprised at reading a nicely rated novel and finding a character that has some depth beyond literal first impressions” – but that’s, sadly, not really the case (not in my experience, anyway).

To be fully transparent, I have zero intention of turning this into a dick-measuring contest and resorting to arguments such as “well, I read/watched/played [X], [Y] and [Z], while you didn’t, so I am automatically more qualified to make objective statements about the quality of fiction than you are”, but I can genuinely count the number of stories I know that could *even remotely* contest with Lessons in Love in terms of the quality of their writing on one hand. Most of the fiction I normally engage with falls somewhere on the spectrum between “good”, “great” or even “outstanding” – and, obviously, there is an equal number of unfortunate examples that belong to the categories of “abysmal”, “bad” or “mediocre” – yet in terms of being directly comparable to LiL, of all things, there are *none*. Now, I fully admit that this evaluation is at least partially dictated by my own personal biases, sure, but even outside of those there is just *way too much* excellence in Selebus’ creation, way too many clever connections, and thematic depth, and clearly visible effort for it all to just be a product of my imagination – and so I will continue to relentlessly argue in LiL’s favor whenever I can, out of pure and selfless love for what I consider to be the work of true art.

Likewise, I strongly resent the implication that the genre of “adult porn games” is somehow inherently different from any other genre of fiction, to the point where it has to be judged on its own separate metrics rather than the same scale we use for everything else. I view Lessons in Love through the same critical lens I view Hermann Hesse’s “Demian”, or Breaking Bad, or Umineko, or any of the games made by Ice-Pick Lodge and Project Moon – and it doesn’t matter that LiL is technically “porn” while all of the other examples I listed aren’t, because my ability/inability to masturbate to a piece of fiction does not affect how I approach it: neither emotionally nor intellectually.

And while I do fundamentally agree with your statement that “enjoyment has nothing to do with quality of writing” – because, yes, subjectivity will *always* trump objectivity in this particular case – as someone who is *extremely* anal about the quality of prose in my text-based media, unimaginative, redundant or badly translated text just immediately takes me out of it.

CharlotteWiltshire26 said:
Yes, I am well aware that these were all things people had issues with – it’s just that, well, I kinda fundamentally disagree with them on that front and don’t really see any of the examples you listed as *actual* flaws in the writing:

– Sensei “becoming a passive protagonist for far too long” makes perfect sense from a writing perspective, because it is entirely consistent with how his character was presented to us beforehand. We *know* that this is just how he reacts to severe emotional loss, so this development doesn’t come out of nowhere – which is exactly why I personally don’t have any issues with it. The game intentionally spends a lot of time in earlier Chapters painting a very unflattering picture of just how much of a trainwreck Akira became after Sekai’s death, and the beginning of Chapter 4 is a direct repeat of that situation – with all that entails – allowing us to witness his mental breakdown firsthand. Now, was it “fun” or “engaging” to watch the guy endlessly mop around or constantly spout depressive and self-deprecating monologues? Perhaps not to everybody. But it *did* allow the narrative to focus on characters *other* than Sensei, to show us how their lives change and develop *beyond* the scope of just their one-on-one interactions with Akira, without his shadow perpetually looming over them – which was, IMO, a fully welcome and beneficial change that only made the story better, not worse. Plus, I hate whenever characters in fiction get back to normal *way* too quickly afer experiencing what is effectively a life-shattering event, so Sensei battling his depression and apathy for the entire Chapter thus far felt both organic and realistic.

– “Abandoning an increasing focus on solving the Reset mysteries” is also a flaw *only* if you approach Lessons in Love from a fairly narrow-minded perspective of “this is explicitly a story about how the characters are trying to find a way to escape the never-ending time loop, and everything else that happens is entirely secondary to that main overarching goal”, which just isn’t true. The Resets are nothing more than a set dressing, a convenient narrative device to facilitate what LiL *actually* is about: exploration of trauma, forbidden relationships, family, personal growth/regression and many other things – in the similar vein of how Umineko isn’t *actually* about “solving the murders” or Homestuck isn’t *actually* about “playing Sburb”. These are all grand, multi-faceted narratives that use relatively simple and easily-understood plot hooks as a simple backdrop to keep you entertained during the earlier parts, until the full brunt of their thematic complexity finally sets in. Besides, the beginning of Chapter 4 was, like, barely 40% into the entirety of LiL, and we’re still just recently passed the approximate halfway point – focusing *too much* on grand narrative revelations regarding Resets at this point in time would have been very premature on Selebus’ part.

– “Shift to unlimited derivation in the form of the god of the week” *could* be pretty jarring/annoying for some people, I’ll admit, but as long as these “Gods of the week” mostly stay in the background in the form of occasional references and one-off appearances rather than become the sole focus of the paranormal side of narrative – which *is* the case as of right now, because Pareidolia, Ami, Nodoka, Sekaori and Nao-chan all individually played a much bigger role in Chapter 4 in terms of the meta-stuff than *all* of the “new Gods” combined – I still maintain that all of this remains in the realm of “subjective preferences” rather than “objective narrative flaw”. Personally, I played Disco Elysium, both Pathologic games and read most of Haruki Murakami’s works – some strange surreal shit just casually happening in the story with zero buildup or fanfare for the sake of “vibes” rather than direct story significance doesn’t faze me in the slightest.

– Full disclosure: I am one of the few rare LiL fans who genuinely enjoys Dorm Wars, so I never really had any issues with the seeming tone dissonance of some of the latest DW installments a lot of people apparently complained about, because it all goes back to my earlier-made point about intentional juxtaposition. The “Sports War” served as a well-needed breath of levity after the depression marathon that was the entire beginning of Chapter 4 (in addition to clearly showcasing how their collective Akira withdrawal slowly causes all of Class 1-A to progressively get more and more unhinged as the days go by), and both Nodokathons always made perfect sense to me in terms of their placement within the narrative: all of the participants had plausible reasons for both being selected by Nodoka and actually choosing to attend, their borderline out-of-character horny behavior could be easily explained by them being permanently hormonal teenagers in the throes of their puberty (I myself once went to a similar “group event” when I was their age, so I have a first-hand experience with how that secretive, intimate atmosphere can easily erode your inhibitions), and Nodoka’s own motives in regards to what she hoped to achieve by organizing Nodokathons have been pretty much openly stated both times, so this wasn’t a random or out-of-character thing for her either.

– NTR shit is stupid, and that’s really all there is to say on the matter.

The dude obviously isn’t perfect – no one is – and when you’re writing a story of LiL’s complexity while *also* being on a severe deadline, some unfortunate mistakes are bound to come up here and there, regardless of how much you try to prevent them – that’s just how it works. – Full disclosure: I am one of the few rare LiL fans who genuinely enjoys Dorm Wars, so I never really had any issues with the seeming tone dissonance of some of the latest DW installments a lot of people apparently complained about, because it all goes back to my earlier-made point about intentional juxtaposition. The “Sports War” served as a well-needed breath of levity after the depression marathon that was the entire beginning of Chapter 4 (in addition to clearly showcasing how their collective Akira withdrawal slowly causes all of Class 1-A to progressively get more and more unhinged as the days go by), and both Nodokathons always made perfect sense to me in terms of their placement within the narrative: all of the participants had plausible reasons for both being selected by Nodoka and actually choosing to attend, their borderline out-of-character horny behavior could be easily explained by them being permanently hormonal teenagers in the throes of their puberty (I myself once went to a similar “group event” when I was their age, so I have a first-hand experience with how that secretive, intimate atmosphere can easily erode your inhibitions), and Nodoka’s own motives in regards to what she hoped to achieve by organizing Nodokathons have been pretty much openly stated both times, so this wasn’t a random or out-of-character thing for her either.

– NTR shit is stupid, and that’s really all there is to say on the matter.

spoilers.title: Further clarifications about my earlier post
spoilers.html:
The specific strength of Selebus’ writing that I was trying to convey in the “Stereotype Subversion” part of my analysis isn’t just “going beyond an initial assumption of a character” – it’s “going beyond an initial assumption of a character in a way that *directly subverts* your original perspective on them *without* it feeling forced or completely out of left field”.

It’s one thing to simply learn a new piece of information that makes all of the seemingly irrelevant details neatly fall into place and finally reveal the full picture – and quite another to suddenly come to a realization that the puzzle you’ve been trying to assemble all this time doesn’t actually exist, and that its pieces, when properly put together, reveal something else entirely. The former *is* just basic good writing, yes, but the latter is not, because it takes much more careful planning and extra care in order to create both an effective/believable “fake front” *and* and an equally fitting/satisfying “truth” that don’t contradict each other in any way, shape or form – without creating a “Logic Error”, in Umineko terms.

Almost all of the counterexamples you bring up about the characters “being who they initially appear to be” are from Chapter 1 or early Chapter 2 – as in, still effectively the beginning part of the story where their “stereotypes” are either still being established or haven’t been fully subverted yet. Can you do the same for the later parts of LiL, though? How many instances are there of Chika still acting like a superficial “basic gyaru”, or Yumi bullying people, or Sana being extremely timid and reserved, or Tsuneyo not properly understanding the implications of what is happening, or Touka behaving like a stereotypical “rich girl” (as well as any other relevant stereotypical traits for the rest of the cast) throughout the second half of Chapter 3 and the entirety of Chapter 4? Maybe you could cherry-pick a few among some of the more light-hearted and comedic scenes, sure, but during the truly serious stuff? Suddenly Makoto no longer cares about following rules or studying, Miku shows actual insight and proactive thinking (like during Maki’s recent 0.55 events), Yasu is sweet and vulnerable rather than creepy and annoying, Otoha is not even remotely “normal”, Kirin’s reaction to Haruka’s advances in 0.54 is a drastic departure from her “unwanted sexual contact – what is that, lol?” line she drops during “Dyed Orange, Drenched in Sun” – etcetera. These are *not* the same archetypical, clearly defined characters that were presented to us during their first five-ten personal events, and the difference here is much greater than the simple “well, I know their trauma now, so that explains everything” – or at least that’s how my schizo brain interprets it.

spoilers.title: General writing discussion
spoilers.html:
Finally, you say “most of the praise for Selebus' writing comes from the fact that it is amazing writing for its genre (adult porn games) – you'd hardly find anyone being surprised at reading a nicely rated novel and finding a character that has some depth beyond literal first impressions” – but that’s, sadly, not really the case (not in my experience, anyway).

To be fully transparent, I have zero intention of turning this into a dick-measuring contest and resorting to arguments such as “well, I read/watched/played [X], [Y] and [Z], while you didn’t, so I am automatically more qualified to make objective statements about the quality of fiction than you are”, but I can genuinely count the number of stories I know that could *even remotely* contest with Lessons in Love in terms of the quality of their writing on one hand. Most of the fiction I normally engage with falls somewhere on the spectrum between “good”, “great” or even “outstanding” – and, obviously, there is an equal number of unfortunate examples that belong to the categories of “abysmal”, “bad” or “mediocre” – yet in terms of being directly comparable to LiL, of all things, there are *none*. Now, I fully admit that this evaluation is at least partially dictated by my own personal biases, sure, but even outside of those there is just *way too much* excellence in Selebus’ creation, way too many clever connections, and thematic depth, and clearly visible effort for it all to just be a product of my imagination – and so I will continue to relentlessly argue in LiL’s favor whenever I can, out of pure and selfless love for what I consider to be the work of true art.

Likewise, I strongly resent the implication that the genre of “adult porn games” is somehow inherently different from any other genre of fiction, to the point where it has to be judged on its own separate metrics rather than the same scale we use for everything else. I view Lessons in Love through the same critical lens I view Hermann Hesse’s “Demian”, or Breaking Bad, or Umineko, or any of the games made by Ice-Pick Lodge and Project Moon – and it doesn’t matter that LiL is technically “porn” while all of the other examples I listed aren’t, because my ability/inability to masturbate to a piece of fiction does not affect how I approach it: neither emotionally nor intellectually.

And while I do fundamentally agree with your statement that “enjoyment has nothing to do with quality of writing” – because, yes, subjectivity will *always* trump objectivity in this particular case – as someone who is *extremely* anal about the quality of prose in my text-based media, unimaginative, redundant or badly translated text just immediately takes me out of it.

truly masterpieces of writing that "aren't inherently different from any other genre of fiction":
LiL is not a novel, thus it can't be judged as a novel alone. The medium through which you consume a story is the story. If you watch a movie, the script doesn't have to describe a scene, you see it with your eyes. It's there. If you play a game, the point is that you, the player, conduct the action - thus there's way less narration and hand-holding, it's supposed to be interactive. If you play an adult game, the action of sex taking the center stage is a given - when not falling into the common category of "collect all cg scenes from all the different characters".

If you don't consider the writing of LiL as an adult game, rather than "any other sort of writing" then you're ignoring the whole point of Selebus creating an adult game rather than writing a novel. Which is fine if you want to say "I'd rather he wrote a novel", but that could be either better or worse, and we don't know how that'd be like - as that is not what LiL is.

Furthermore, if you want to talk about connecting to the story on a personal level, that is up to each one. But what you put forward is that LiL is nearly flawless in terms of writing and that you disagree with most of its criticisms. That your post was supposed to provide "concrete and convincing examples that Selebus cares about his writing, and that it is successful because of him, rathen than in spite of him". Was that ever in doubt?
I chose to comment solely on this part of your post because, honestly, I don't think there's anything productive to say about anything else. Your love for the game is quite clear and, genuinely, I'd advise you to join the LiL discord. I think you could thrive there.

CharlotteWiltshire26 said:
Yes, I am well aware that these were all things people had issues with – it’s just that, well, I kinda fundamentally disagree with them on that front and don’t really see any of the examples you listed as *actual* flaws in the writing:

– Sensei “becoming a passive protagonist for far too long” makes perfect sense from a writing perspective, because it is entirely consistent with how his character was presented to us beforehand. We *know* that this is just how he reacts to severe emotional loss, so this development doesn’t come out of nowhere – which is exactly why I personally don’t have any issues with it. The game intentionally spends a lot of time in earlier Chapters painting a very unflattering picture of just how much of a trainwreck Akira became after Sekai’s death, and the beginning of Chapter 4 is a direct repeat of that situation – with all that entails – allowing us to witness his mental breakdown firsthand. Now, was it “fun” or “engaging” to watch the guy endlessly mop around or constantly spout depressive and self-deprecating monologues? Perhaps not to everybody. But it *did* allow the narrative to focus on characters *other* than Sensei, to show us how their lives change and develop *beyond* the scope of just their one-on-one interactions with Akira, without his shadow perpetually looming over them – which was, IMO, a fully welcome and beneficial change that only made the story better, not worse. Plus, I hate whenever characters in fiction get back to normal *way* too quickly afer experiencing what is effectively a life-shattering event, so Sensei battling his depression and apathy for the entire Chapter thus far felt both organic and realistic.

– “Abandoning an increasing focus on solving the Reset mysteries” is also a flaw *only* if you approach Lessons in Love from a fairly narrow-minded perspective of “this is explicitly a story about how the characters are trying to find a way to escape the never-ending time loop, and everything else that happens is entirely secondary to that main overarching goal”, which just isn’t true. The Resets are nothing more than a set dressing, a convenient narrative device to facilitate what LiL *actually* is about: exploration of trauma, forbidden relationships, family, personal growth/regression and many other things – in the similar vein of how Umineko isn’t *actually* about “solving the murders” or Homestuck isn’t *actually* about “playing Sburb”. These are all grand, multi-faceted narratives that use relatively simple and easily-understood plot hooks as a simple backdrop to keep you entertained during the earlier parts, until the full brunt of their thematic complexity finally sets in. Besides, the beginning of Chapter 4 was, like, barely 40% into the entirety of LiL, and we’re still just recently passed the approximate halfway point – focusing *too much* on grand narrative revelations regarding Resets at this point in time would have been very premature on Selebus’ part.

– “Shift to unlimited derivation in the form of the god of the week” *could* be pretty jarring/annoying for some people, I’ll admit, but as long as these “Gods of the week” mostly stay in the background in the form of occasional references and one-off appearances rather than become the sole focus of the paranormal side of narrative – which *is* the case as of right now, because Pareidolia, Ami, Nodoka, Sekaori and Nao-chan all individually played a much bigger role in Chapter 4 in terms of the meta-stuff than *all* of the “new Gods” combined – I still maintain that all of this remains in the realm of “subjective preferences” rather than “objective narrative flaw”. Personally, I played Disco Elysium, both Pathologic games and read most of Haruki Murakami’s works – some strange surreal shit just casually happening in the story with zero buildup or fanfare for the sake of “vibes” rather than direct story significance doesn’t faze me in the slightest.

– Full disclosure: I am one of the few rare LiL fans who genuinely enjoys Dorm Wars, so I never really had any issues with the seeming tone dissonance of some of the latest DW installments a lot of people apparently complained about, because it all goes back to my earlier-made point about intentional juxtaposition. The “Sports War” served as a well-needed breath of levity after the depression marathon that was the entire beginning of Chapter 4 (in addition to clearly showcasing how their collective Akira withdrawal slowly causes all of Class 1-A to progressively get more and more unhinged as the days go by), and both Nodokathons always made perfect sense to me in terms of their placement within the narrative: all of the participants had plausible reasons for both being selected by Nodoka and actually choosing to attend, their borderline out-of-character horny behavior could be easily explained by them being permanently hormonal teenagers in the throes of their puberty (I myself once went to a similar “group event” when I was their age, so I have a first-hand experience with how that secretive, intimate atmosphere can easily erode your inhibitions), and Nodoka’s own motives in regards to what she hoped to achieve by organizing Nodokathons have been pretty much openly stated both times, so this wasn’t a random or out-of-character thing for her either.

– NTR shit is stupid, and that’s really all there is to say on the matter.

– As for the inconsistencies… well, it’s hard to say for sure – perhaps you are right. I never implied that Selebus is *infallible*, however – only that he is really, really good at what he does. The dude obviously isn’t perfect – no one is – and when you’re writing a story of LiL’s complexity while *also* being on a severe deadline, some unfortunate mistakes are bound to come up here and there, regardless of how much you try to prevent them – that’s just how it works. I’m not excusing these “retcons” (if that’s what they are, of course), but rather pointing out that – in my opinion, anyway – they are relatively small flaws in an otherwise almost flawless narrative, and that, when judged as a writer, Selebus deserves a lot more praise for his successes than condemnation of his failures. You disagreeing with me on Lessons in Love being anywhere near “flawless” is fine – I wholeheartedly respect your opinion – but that’s just how I see it, plain and simple.

The specific strength of Selebus’ writing that I was trying to convey in the “Stereotype Subversion” part of my analysis isn’t just “going beyond an initial assumption of a character” – it’s “going beyond an initial assumption of a character in a way that *directly subverts* your original perspective on them *without* it feeling forced or completely out of left field”.

It’s one thing to simply learn a new piece of information that makes all of the seemingly irrelevant details neatly fall into place and finally reveal the full picture – and quite another to suddenly come to a realization that the puzzle you’ve been trying to assemble all this time doesn’t actually exist, and that its pieces, when properly put together, reveal something else entirely. The former *is* just basic good writing, yes, but the latter is not, because it takes much more careful planning and extra care in order to create both an effective/believable “fake front” *and* and an equally fitting/satisfying “truth” that don’t contradict each other in any way, shape or form – without creating a “Logic Error”, in Umineko terms.

Almost all of the counterexamples you bring up about the characters “being who they initially appear to be” are from Chapter 1 or early Chapter 2 – as in, still effectively the beginning part of the story where their “stereotypes” are either still being established or haven’t been fully subverted yet. Can you do the same for the later parts of LiL, though? How many instances are there of Chika still acting like a superficial “basic gyaru”, or Yumi bullying people, or Sana being extremely timid and reserved, or Tsuneyo not properly understanding the implications of what is happening, or Touka behaving like a stereotypical “rich girl” (as well as any other relevant stereotypical traits for the rest of the cast) throughout the second half of Chapter 3 and the entirety of Chapter 4? Maybe you could cherry-pick a few among some of the more light-hearted and comedic scenes, sure, but during the truly serious stuff? Suddenly Makoto no longer cares about following rules or studying, Miku shows actual insight and proactive thinking (like during Maki’s recent 0.55 events), Yasu is sweet and vulnerable rather than creepy and annoying, Otoha is not even remotely “normal”, Kirin’s reaction to Haruka’s advances in 0.54 is a drastic departure from her “unwanted sexual contact – what is that, lol?” line she drops during “Dyed Orange, Drenched in Sun” – etcetera. These are *not* the same archetypical, clearly defined characters that were presented to us during their first five-ten personal events, and the difference here is much greater than the simple “well, I know their trauma now, so that explains everything” – or at least that’s how my schizo brain interprets it.

Finally, you say “most of the praise for Selebus' writing comes from the fact that it is amazing writing for its genre (adult porn games) – you'd hardly find anyone being surprised at reading a nicely rated novel and finding a character that has some depth beyond literal first impressions” – but that’s, sadly, not really the case (not in my experience, anyway).

To be fully transparent, I have zero intention of turning this into a dick-measuring contest and resorting to arguments such as “well, I read/watched/played [X], [Y] and [Z], while you didn’t, so I am automatically more qualified to make objective statements about the quality of fiction than you are”, but I can genuinely count the number of stories I know that could *even remotely* contest with Lessons in Love in terms of the quality of their writing on one hand. Most of the fiction I normally engage with falls somewhere on the spectrum between “good”, “great” or even “outstanding” – and, obviously, there is an equal number of unfortunate examples that belong to the categories of “abysmal”, “bad” or “mediocre” – yet in terms of being directly comparable to LiL, of all things, there are *none*. Now, I fully admit that this evaluation is at least partially dictated by my own personal biases, sure, but even outside of those there is just *way too much* excellence in Selebus’ creation, way too many clever connections, and thematic depth, and clearly visible effort for it all to just be a product of my imagination – and so I will continue to relentlessly argue in LiL’s favor whenever I can, out of pure and selfless love for what I consider to be the work of true art.

Likewise, I strongly resent the implication that the genre of “adult porn games” is somehow inherently different from any other genre of fiction, to the point where it has to be judged on its own separate metrics rather than the same scale we use for everything else. I view Lessons in Love through the same critical lens I view Hermann Hesse’s “Demian”, or Breaking Bad, or Umineko, or any of the games made by Ice-Pick Lodge and Project Moon – and it doesn’t matter that LiL is technically “porn” while all of the other examples I listed aren’t, because my ability/inability to masturbate to a piece of fiction does not affect how I approach it: neither emotionally nor intellectually.

And while I do fundamentally agree with your statement that “enjoyment has nothing to do with quality of writing” – because, yes, subjectivity will *always* trump objectivity in this particular case – as someone who is *extremely* anal about the quality of prose in my text-based media, unimaginative, redundant or badly translated text just immediately takes me out of it.

spoilers.text:
Yes, I am well aware that these were all things people had issues with – it’s just that, well, I kinda fundamentally disagree with them on that front and don’t really see any of the examples you listed as *actual* flaws in the writing:
– Sensei “becoming a passive protagonist for far too long” makes perfect sense from a writing perspective, because it is entirely consistent with how his character was presented to us beforehand. We *know* that this is just how he reacts to severe emotional loss, so this development doesn’t come out of nowhere – which is exactly why I personally don’t have any issues with it. The game intentionally spends a lot of time in earlier Chapters painting a very unflattering picture of just how much of a trainwreck Akira became after Sekai’s death, and the beginning of Chapter 4 is a direct repeat of that situation – with all that entails – allowing us to witness his mental breakdown firsthand. Now, was it “fun” or “engaging” to watch the guy endlessly mop around or constantly spout depressive and self-deprecating monologues? Perhaps not to everybody. But it *did* allow the narrative to focus on characters *other* than Sensei, to show us how their lives change and develop *beyond* the scope of just their one-on-one interactions with Akira, without his shadow perpetually looming over them – which was, IMO, a fully welcome and beneficial change that only made the story better, not worse. Plus, I hate whenever characters in fiction get back to normal *way* too quickly afer experiencing what is effectively a life-shattering event, so Sensei battling his depression and apathy for the entire Chapter thus far felt both organic and realistic.
– “Abandoning an increasing focus on solving the Reset mysteries” is also a flaw *only* if you approach Lessons in Love from a fairly narrow-minded perspective of “this is explicitly a story about how the characters are trying to find a way to escape the never-ending time loop, and everything else that happens is entirely secondary to that main overarching goal”, which just isn’t true. The Resets are nothing more than a set dressing, a convenient narrative device to facilitate what LiL *actually* is about: exploration of trauma, forbidden relationships, family, personal growth/regression and many other things – in the similar vein of how Umineko isn’t *actually* about “solving the murders” or Homestuck isn’t *actually* about “playing Sburb”. These are all grand, multi-faceted narratives that use relatively simple and easily-understood plot hooks as a simple backdrop to keep you entertained during the earlier parts, until the full brunt of their thematic complexity finally sets in. Besides, the beginning of Chapter 4 was, like, barely 40% into the entirety of LiL, and we’re still just recently passed the approximate halfway point – focusing *too much* on grand narrative revelations regarding Resets at this point in time would have been very premature on Selebus’ part.
– “Shift to unlimited derivation in the form of the god of the week” *could* be pretty jarring/annoying for some people, I’ll admit, but as long as these “Gods of the week” mostly stay in the background in the form of occasional references and one-off appearances rather than become the sole focus of the paranormal side of narrative – which *is* the case as of right now, because Pareidolia, Ami, Nodoka, Sekaori and Nao-chan all individually played a much bigger role in Chapter 4 in terms of the meta-stuff than *all* of the “new Gods” combined – I still maintain that all of this remains in the realm of “subjective preferences” rather than “objective narrative flaw”. Personally, I played Disco Elysium, both Pathologic games and read most of Haruki Murakami’s works – some strange surreal shit just casually happening in the story with zero buildup or fanfare for the sake of “vibes” rather than direct story significance doesn’t faze me in the slightest.
– Full disclosure: I am one of the few rare LiL fans who genuinely enjoys Dorm Wars, so I never really had any issues with the seeming tone dissonance of some of the latest DW installments a lot of people apparently complained about, because it all goes back to my earlier-made point about intentional juxtaposition. The “Sports War” served as a well-needed breath of levity after the depression marathon that was the entire beginning of Chapter 4 (in addition to clearly showcasing how their collective Akira withdrawal slowly causes all of Class 1-A to progressively get more and more unhinged as the days go by), and both Nodokathons always made perfect sense to me in terms of their placement within the narrative: all of the participants had plausible reasons for both being selected by Nodoka and actually choosing to attend, their borderline out-of-character horny behavior could be easily explained by them being permanently hormonal teenagers in the throes of their puberty (I myself once went to a similar “group event” when I was their age, so I have a first-hand experience with how that secretive, intimate atmosphere can easily erode your inhibitions), and Nodoka’s own motives in regards to what she hoped to achieve by organizing Nodokathons have been pretty much openly stated both times, so this wasn’t a random or out-of-character thing for her either.
– NTR shit is stupid, and that’s really all there is to say on the matter.
– As for the inconsistencies… well, it’s hard to say for sure – perhaps you are right. I never implied that Selebus is *infallible*, however – only that he is really, really good at what he does. The dude obviously isn’t perfect – no one is – and when you’re writing a story of LiL’s complexity while *also* being on a severe deadline, some unfortunate mistakes are bound to come up here and there, regardless of how much you try to prevent them – that’s just how it works. I’m not excusing these “retcons” (if that’s what they are, of course), but rather pointing out that – in my opinion, anyway – they are relatively small flaws in an otherwise almost flawless narrative, and that, when judged as a writer, Selebus deserves a lot more praise for his successes than condemnation of his failures. You disagreeing with me on Lessons in Love being anywhere near “flawless” is fine – I wholeheartedly respect your opinion – but that’s just how I see it, plain and simple.

spoilers.title: Further clarifications about my earlier post
spoilers.html:
The specific strength of Selebus’ writing that I was trying to convey in the “Stereotype Subversion” part of my analysis isn’t just “going beyond an initial assumption of a character” – it’s “going beyond an initial assumption of a character in a way that *directly subverts* your original perspective on them *without* it feeling forced or completely out of left field”.

It’s one thing to simply learn a new piece of information that makes all of the seemingly irrelevant details neatly fall into place and finally reveal the full picture – and quite another to suddenly come to a realization that the puzzle you’ve been trying to assemble all this time doesn’t actually exist, and that its pieces, when properly put together, reveal something else entirely. The former *is* just basic good writing, yes, but the latter is not, because it takes much more careful planning and extra care in order to create both an effective/believable “fake front” *and* and an equally fitting/satisfying “truth” that don’t contradict each other in any way, shape or form – without creating a “Logic Error”, in Umineko terms.

Almost all of the counterexamples you bring up about the characters “being who they initially appear to be” are from Chapter 1 or early Chapter 2 – as in, still effectively the beginning part of the story where their “stereotypes” are either still being established or haven’t been fully subverted yet. Can you do the same for the later parts of LiL, though? How many instances are there of Chika still acting like a superficial “basic gyaru”, or Yumi bullying people, or Sana being extremely timid and reserved, or Tsuneyo not properly understanding the implications of what is happening, or Touka behaving like a stereotypical “rich girl” (as well as any other relevant stereotypical traits for the rest of the cast) throughout the second half of Chapter 3 and the entirety of Chapter 4? Maybe you could cherry-pick a few among some of the more light-hearted and comedic scenes, sure, but during the truly serious stuff? Suddenly Makoto no longer cares about following rules or studying, Miku shows actual insight and proactive thinking (like during Maki’s recent 0.55 events), Yasu is sweet and vulnerable rather than creepy and annoying, Otoha is not even remotely “normal”, Kirin’s reaction to Haruka’s advances in 0.54 is a drastic departure from her “unwanted sexual contact – what is that, lol?” line she drops during “Dyed Orange, Drenched in Sun” – etcetera. These are *not* the same archetypical, clearly defined characters that were presented to us during their first five-ten personal events, and the difference here is much greater than the simple “well, I know their trauma now, so that explains everything” – or at least that’s how my schizo brain interprets it.

spoilers.title: General writing discussion
spoilers.html:
Finally, you say “most of the praise for Selebus' writing comes from the fact that it is amazing writing for its genre (adult porn games) – you'd hardly find anyone being surprised at reading a nicely rated novel and finding a character that has some depth beyond literal first impressions” – but that’s, sadly, not really the case (not in my experience, anyway).

To be fully transparent, I have zero intention of turning this into a dick-measuring contest and resorting to arguments such as “well, I read/watched/played [X], [Y] and [Z], while you didn’t, so I am automatically more qualified to make objective statements about the quality of fiction than you are”, but I can genuinely count the number of stories I know that could *even remotely* contest with Lessons in Love in terms of the quality of their writing on one hand. Most of the fiction I normally engage with falls somewhere on the spectrum between “good”, “great” or even “outstanding” – and, obviously, there is an equal number of unfortunate examples that belong to the categories of “abysmal”, “bad” or “mediocre” – yet in terms of being directly comparable to LiL, of all things, there are *none*. Now, I fully admit that this evaluation is at least partially dictated by my own personal biases, sure, but even outside of those there is just *way too much* excellence in Selebus’ creation, way too many clever connections, and thematic depth, and clearly visible effort for it all to just be a product of my imagination – and so I will continue to relentlessly argue in LiL’s favor whenever I can, out of pure and selfless love for what I consider to be the work of true art.

Likewise, I strongly resent the implication that the genre of “adult porn games” is somehow inherently different from any other genre of fiction, to the point where it has to be judged on its own separate metrics rather than the same scale we use for everything else. I view Lessons in Love through the same critical lens I view Hermann Hesse’s “Demian”, or Breaking Bad, or Umineko, or any of the games made by Ice-Pick Lodge and Project Moon – and it doesn’t matter that LiL is technically “porn” while all of the other examples I listed aren’t, because my ability/inability to masturbate to a piece of fiction does not affect how I approach it: neither emotionally nor intellectually.

And while I do fundamentally agree with your statement that “enjoyment has nothing to do with quality of writing” – because, yes, subjectivity will *always* trump objectivity in this particular case – as someone who is *extremely* anal about the quality of prose in my text-based media, unimaginative, redundant or badly translated text just immediately takes me out of it.

Ways to prepare coffee:

Pour over coffee is an antique technique, dating back to Melitta Bentz’s prototypes more than a hundred years ago.

Pour over, aka hand drip coffee, has had a huge renaissance in recent years.

It all began when Hario V60 suddenly came out of nowhere and became the brewer of choice in many specialty coffee shops in the US and Europe.

While the West had largely dismissed the minimalist pour over approach, it had flourished and developed in Japan, where Hario is from.

Since then, many other Japanese brands have entered the market and cut out a slice for themselves: Kalita, Origami, Cafec, Munieq, and Kono, just to mention a few.

Pour over coffee seems simple, which it also is to a certain degree, but at the same time, it has the potential to be a complicated and nuanced brewing method.

posts.content_html_raw:
Okay guys, may I ask for some spoilers from anyone who knows more about this?

I’ve only played around 3 to 4 hours so far and haven’t reached any major scenes, yet, I can’t really complain, because the narrative quality is surprisingly strong. It strongly reminds me of old-school non-eroge visual novels due to how immersive the storytelling is, and because of that, the game feels somewhat off as an eroge.

So here are my questions:

1. From the very first meeting, Maya seems to hint that she is trapped in a loop. If that is the case, does the game ever mention how many times she has already gone through that loop?

2. Was the "old sensei" actually the real one, or was he also an imitation like the "new sensei"? If so, does the game ever explain any differences in their personality?

3. Futaba, or the girl who shares a room with the jirai-kei styled girl, is she actually overweight or already pregnant?

This might sound odd, but I have an instinct related to the “level” at which someone would start being bullied for their body. I was bullied in the past for being too skinny, so I tend to be sensitive to this kind of thing. With Futaba, that instinct feels off, because judging purely from her appearance, her proportions do not seem to match the reason given for the bullying. If she is meant to be overweight, is this due to Koikatsu limitations, or is there another explanation?

4. Are all the heroines in this game completely messed up, with none of them being "healthy" at all? From the three characters who visit the MC’s house, all of them seem to carry very heavy issues. I understand that the game has a horror tag, but if there is not a single character who can be considered "healthy", it slightly reduces immersion.

5. Is the “war against aliens” context necessary for anything beyond explaining why there are fewer men on Earth? Is this explored further in the story?

6. Lastly, is the ending of this game already planned? Has the developer mentioned anything, or is there any implicit information in the game itself? It would be a shame if there is only one true ending. I personally hope that destroying the world is one possible outcome, whether as a form of mercy killing (like “freeing” Maya from an endless loop), or driven by frustration (such as being exhausted from dying repeatedly or eventually longing to go home)), or simply the objective was already completed decides to destroy it, similar to the genocide routes in Undertale.


I never expected to think this seriously about plot in eroge I just started, but here we are.

And if this sounds AI-generated, that is because I did ask an AI for help translating it. I can understand English passively, listening and reading are fine, but I struggle when I need to respond or start a conversation.


I would really appreciate any responses and thank you in advance for any answers.

Thanks for the response.
  1. About the answer to the first question, it felt a bit lacking in detail, but I get why. It’s probably better to figure these things out on my own since too much explanation can can mess with immersion . Personally, I was hoping that at some point she actually counted the loops, then stopped doing it because it felt pointless. If the story doesn’t go that way, then I guess we’ll see where the plot ends up.

    That said, it’s kind of unfortunate. A game with this level of immersive storytelling feels way better when you can sit still and play for long stretches. Because of my health right now, I’m forced to move around a lot, change positions, and deal with constant nausea. That’s why I asked for spoilers in the first place—my immersion is already broken by having to move my body so often.

  2. About the sensei, this question came up because Ami describes the sensei as “strange” mostly due to memory loss. But we know that the current sensei is a new sensei, which makes me wonder whether this version actually has no inherent personality issues at all.
    If the new sensei doesn’t remember the current world, but still has motivations and goals that are different from the old sensei, then it feels weird that both versions interact with the heroines in such similar ways. That made me think: maybe the sensei was always the same entity, just split across different timelines? If that’s the case, what could have triggered that change?

    This question got even stronger when Maya revealed that she already knew we were the new sensei. So thanks for confirming that. No need to add more spoilers—I’d rather see the rest myself. I just hope the second question actually gets answered later, and if it does, i hope dev execute it very well.

  3. About Futaba, it was honestly refreshing to see body dysmorphia shown from a different cultural perspective. It proofing my own instinct doesn’t really apply to the developer’s cultural context, which is an interesting lesson in itself. Where I’m from, a body like hers wouldn’t realistically be bullied. It would need to be much bigger. Some people might argue it’s because she’s a woman, but even then, her proportions wouldn’t really be enough to trigger weight-based bullying here. That said, this is obviously subjective.

    But if the story explains that Futaba’s current body, despite her being thin in past, is caused by those two conditions, and that she goes through repeated cycles of gaining and losing weight because of them, then this game would easily be one of the most interesting takes on body dysmorphia I’ve seen. That kind of vicious cycle does happen in real life. It’s rare, but definitely not unrealistic.

  4. About the neurotic angle, yeah, I get it. One of the reasons I downloaded this game was because I saw discussions about a heroine who “has trouble understanding emotions”—not cognitively, but actually feeling them. If I remember correctly, the name is nodoka ?

    I really want to see how her story plays out. Like, would she actively manipulate situations or people just to understand the emotions involved? Is she reflective, or prone to self-contemplation? And if she does those things, is it driven by morality, or just methodology? Please don’t answer that—I want to experience Nodoka’s route firsthand.

    When Ami briefs the sensei about the world, the neurotic vibe is very noticeable, and that’s when this question first came up. It would be a shame if the sensei never encounters even a single heroine who’s genuinely “healthy.” Sure, everyone has problems, but there are also people who handle them really well and stay stable.

Okay guys, may I ask for some spoilers from anyone who knows more about this?

So here are my questions:

1. From the very first meeting, Maya seems to hint that she is trapped in a loop. If that is the case, does the game ever mention how many times she has already gone through that loop?

2. Was the "old sensei" actually the real one, or was he also an imitation like the "new sensei"? If so, does the game ever explain any differences in their personality?

3. Futaba, or the girl who shares a room with the jirai-kei styled girl, is she actually overweight or already pregnant?

This might sound odd, but I have an instinct related to the “level” at which someone would start being bullied for their body. I was bullied in the past for being too skinny, so I tend to be sensitive to this kind of thing. With Futaba, that instinct feels off, because judging purely from her appearance, her proportions do not seem to match the reason given for the bullying. If she is meant to be overweight, is this due to Koikatsu limitations, or is there another explanation?

4. Are all the heroines in this game completely messed up, with none of them being "healthy" at all? From the three characters who visit the MC’s house, all of them seem to carry very heavy issues. I understand that the game has a horror tag, but if there is not a single character who can be considered "healthy", it slightly reduces immersion.

5. Is the “war against aliens” context necessary for anything beyond explaining why there are fewer men on Earth? Is this explored further in the story?

6. Lastly, is the ending of this game already planned? Has the developer mentioned anything, or is there any implicit information in the game itself? It would be a shame if there is only one true ending. I personally hope that destroying the world is one possible outcome, whether as a form of mercy killing (like “freeing” Maya from an endless loop), or driven by frustration (such as being exhausted from dying repeatedly or eventually longing to go home)), or simply the objective was already completed decides to destroy it, similar to the genocide routes in Undertale.


I never expected to think this seriously about plot in eroge I just started, but here we are.

And if this sounds AI-generated, that is because I did ask an AI for help translating it. I can understand English passively, listening and reading are fine, but I struggle when I need to respond or start a conversation.


I would really appreciate any responses and thank you in advance for any answers.

1) A potentially near-infinite number of times
2) A potentially near-infinite number of Senseis
3) Her brokenness stems from body image issues

6) We have rough roadmap, a harem phase, which we're nearing the end of, a comparitively brief "dark" phase, then up to 36 endings, a "pure" ending for each of the girls, then a "true" ending unlocked after all of the pure endings.

posts.content_html_raw:
I think that Nodoka, along with most characters written by Selebus, is on the edge of "it can all be justified if you try" and "some things could have been written better".
There is a bit of a disconnect between her actions (especially with Yumi and general Yuritopia) from when she's first introduced, to her later actions regarding the "conspiracy theory" arc, "martyr" arc, and current arc. Again, it's not to the extent of it not making sense, but it is a bit of a disconnect.

Would a broken person struggling to recall her messages to herself from over a thousand different timelines, all together in an effort to break the cycle and free them all, in a desperate attempt to not end up like her mother, actually care about Yumi? or lesbians, in general?

It's up to personal taste, I guess. If you think about it, Nodoka could have been written to be either the good Ami or the competent Maya. Instead, she's written to be getting random (and convenient) pieces of information when Selebus wishes her to. One would assume she cares about Futaba, Yumi and lesbians because she doesn't have the full picture most of the time. What would be the point of caring about the latest iteration of what Yumi did to Futaba otherwise?

But then, are all her actions henceforth trying to break the world? Isn't that just a convenient excuse to have her do the most fucked up shit all the time? How many times has she published this book? How many times has she found out about Io? How many times has she answered those impossible questions during the dormwars, to the point where she simply remembers all the answers? This is also worsened by the fact that Nodoka gets her messages directly from Selebus, our other oracle (Yasu) at least gets them from in-game gods.

At the end of the day, by the nature of the game with the thousand cycles and a character that sometimes remembers some of it, I think anything related to her actions can be explained. But if the player still feels like she's either a self-insert, or gets taken out of the story because of how she's portrayed, maybe it ultimately failed?

And this also begs the question: wouldn't it feel better for Akira to be the active investigator of the mysteries of the world instead of her? Were I to write LiL, Nodoka's introduction would veer more into a Noriko like character, just, instead of romantic obsession, she'd endanger him by offering answers, fixated on Akira shortly after they first meet because maybe she remembers something about him. She'd be a foil to Yasu, providing a path through deduction instead of dogma. And both of them would, in turn, be a foil to Maya, that'd preach ignorance for his own safety (at that point in time).
Anyway, I'm fine with Nodoka as it is, mostly because of the gospel of John "Greater love has no one than this: to lay down one's life for one's friends".

There is a bit of a disconnect between her actions (especially with Yumi and general Yuritopia) from when she's first introduced, to her later actions regarding the "conspiracy theory" arc, "martyr" arc, and current arc. Click to expand...
Yeah I was thinking about this a bit in my latest playthrough. I also just don't feel like her characterisation entirely lines up. Her personality in general kind of just flatlines and her attachment to Futaba comes across as completely vapid in light of later events - though arguably that might not be an inconsistency but just her not really caring as much as she says she does early in the game but either way it doesn't really line up with the whole tragic martyr thing that seems to be unfurling.

You can kind of square her just "knowing things" and some of her zanier actions like Nodokathon 2.0 using the meta-narrative but I don't find that a reasonable explanation for what she did to Yumi either so it makes the whole chain just feel malicious and pointless to me.

And as far as her portrayal in the meta-narrative yeah, she does take me out of the story a little bit. She's honestly the weak link of the game for me, there's a couple other characters who have grown somewhat tired for me (namely Futaba and Miku) but Nodoka's the one character I pretty much just skim through completely on my replays specifically because some of her events suck me out of it, not only do her exposition dumps have (seemingly) no explanation but they feel completely unearned and at times out of place.

She's not special nor does she have protection. Imagine what that'd do to a person - it'd be enough to drive them insane for sure. Especially cause she's not Yasu, she can't just default to "well, god knows best and will reveal whatever's necessary to me".

So I think her perception of reality would be warped from that alone. Try to recall Makoto's reaction to the reality of the resets, and how everything became irrelevant to an extent. Well, Makoto was lucky to have that revealed to her - Nodoka is ever trying to reach those revelations and having them taken from her. So I interpret her episodes as culminations of always being on the edge of discovering things, which doubles as trying to recall things she already knew.

I think that'd make an excellent tragic heroine to be honest - if you take that alone, Nodoka is Okabe from Steins;Gate, but with a very faulty reading steiner (ability that makes him able to recall alternate realities). It's just that Selebus didn't choose that for her.

All of this being said, let's examine the other half of Nodoka: her mother. Kyoko had something happen to her, and Nodoka is really scared of becoming just like her. She has no other family, and Kyoko is well, not exactly a vegetable, but at least unresponsive. What does that mean to a child?

Kyoko would have been the one to raise Nodoka - but how would she be even able to do this? Even if we assume that Kyoko was relatively well during her younger years, Nodoka's formation years would be with an unresponsive mother that she has to take care of. If we compare her to Ami, for all that Sekai was, she was deeply caring for Ami. So even if Ami's upbringing was also a tragedy due to the accident + Akira, Nodoka's was conceivably worse.

No human affection to speak of, having to take care of your one relative from an early age, already involved with the resets bullshit from WAY BEFORE terminal 23 (since Kyoko's stuff is from a previous world), I think it'd be kind of weird if Nodoka didn't turn out as she did.

Obsessed with unraveling mysteries that everyone else is unable to even conceive, that she's almost sure is true due to Kyoko and later her own previous selves, terrified of failing just as her mother... At the same time with no emotional concept of what a healthy relationship is like, her most treasured link being that of an unresponsive person, why would she treat relationships in any other way than being it all up to her judgement?

It all makes sense to me. Obviously none of this justifies her behavior towards others, but it does make sense. It's not her ego that dictates that people are below her and can't understand what she's doing, that's the factual truth because of supernatural phenomena.

The issues come, in my mind, when Selebus doesn't bring all of this together, as I have pointed out in previous posts. Almost none of what I have noted is said explicitly in the game. Why not have a scene of Nodoka justifying her actions towards Futaba by her not being able to understand, and have Futaba understanding and still condemning her? "Mille crepe" could have been this.

Why not have a scene of Nodoka being cruel to either Yumi, or Io, or whoever and have her say that she was indeed trying to break the world? (this would be welcomed especially regarding the whole book thing). Why not have her go in the other extreme and say that she was cruel because Yumi deserved it and that it ultimately didn't matter because of the resets, and have another character come in with (Futaba or Ayane would be great for this) "but Nodoka, reset or not, you chose to be cruel. The fact that it repeats just means that when you were free of lasting consequence you revealed yourself to be a cruel person".

I think there was a lot of potential that was ignored in terms of tying up previous setups and making them a big moment. Also that, again, for all that I love LiL, I am a very different writer than Selebus and simply would have done things differently. It's great that he can dish out great content without planning, but I'm a strong believer that at the very least you should have an idea of the big points of each character's arcs so that you can properly convey the low moments, high moments and payoffs. Especially if you're publishing your content before reaching the end.

I also had a fairly negative reaction when I first experienced that scene – though not due to any moral/ethical considerations, but simply because it felt like it came completely out of left field and just didn’t fit with how Lessons in Love usually handles similar topics (with a hefty dose of subtlety and nuance) – yet, after ruminating on it for a couple of days and desperately trying to narratively justify the existence of “When I Say Jump” in my mind, I believe that I *did* ultimately come to understand Selebus’ intention in regards to that event and why showing Yuki’s "downfall" in full was thematically necessary and not just a meaningless “torture porn” for the sake of base-level shock value.

The general consensus at the time (and perhaps still now), if I’m not mistaken, seemed to be that both “When I Say Jump” and Yuki’s subsequent rescue by Tsubasa were a clear set-up for a future “revenge arc” of some kind where Yuki eventually returns to the Yamaguchi Clan and punishes them for what they did to her – which is why the later plot development of Tsubasa just basically solving that entire issue off-screen felt so jarring and anticlimactic to so many people, because they were expecting some great triumphant catharsis and instead got one line of dialogue. I, meanwhile, found it to be perfectly reasonable and thematically consistent, because it fell completely in-line with my personal expectations in regards to where that entire storyline is going to go:

Think back on Yuki’s entire situation prior to “When I Say Jump” and how it was as close to rock-fucking-bottom as we’ve seen for pretty much *any* character in LiL, bar none. Yuki had *literally nothing* to go on: no money (due to spending all of her already meager savings on getting drugs), no hope for the future (due to both cancer *and* her relapse, which squandered all of the progress she managed to make over the years) and no people to support her (because she intentionally tried to alienate anyone close to her and dismantle all of these personal relationships one-by-one). The only thing remaining was her completely empty and meaningless pride as “the Dragon” – something that Yuki only *says* she abandoned, despite it still clearly dictating most of her thoughts and behavior (as she herself points out to Yumi in “The Road to Recovery”: how it “feels nice” to use the Yamaguchi family name when it benefits them, but then shit-talk the yakuza and the Yamaguchi patriarch himself the very next second) – which is exactly why “When I Say Jump” was needed: to mercilessly tear down that delusional pride of hers and bring Yuki to an *actual* rock-bottom – because at that point there is nowhere else to go but *up*.

If you replay that event and pay close attention to what the narration says in regards to Yuki’s inner thoughts while she is getting raped, you’ll notice that her mindset slowly devolves from the original “do not resist, do not fight back – just persist, endure, like you’ve always done it” to a much more basic, desperate feeling of “survive, just survive, no matter the cost”:

“She wasn’t even thinking about the money anymore. She was just glad to be alive – if even for a moment longer.”

is a direct quote from the final scene of that event, clearly demonstrating how there was *nothing* inside Yuki by the point she was thrown outside into the rain – nothing except a singular deep, primal desire to *live*, reignited through pain and desperation after she already had all but completely given up on life. The woman went through a raging purifying fire and emerged victorious: abused and degraded, but unbroken, having gained a new unyielding resolve – and the World responded to that resolve by granting her a literal miracle in the form of an old friend.

In the span of mere hours, Yuki’s life turned around as rapidly as it went downhill: suddenly she was reunited with a dear figure from her long-abandoned past – a figure who, through her immense wealth and vast connections, *also* brought alongside her a possibility of salvation from a previously thought-to-be incurable affliction and an actual hope for a proper future. This is the type of shit that makes people start believing in God IRL: a clearest possible example of a “second chance” and an opportunity to start a new, better life with no prior ties or sins holding you back – so why the fuck would Yuki *ever* decide to just throw it all away and go back for the sake of “revenge” or some shit?

She has finally made a choice to stop mentally associating herself with the yakuza once and for all: no longer “Yuki the Dragon, wife of Yoshitsugu Yamaguchi” (regardless how much he hated him) but just “Yuki the person”, a thirty-something recovering addict who works in a small bar and has friends and family who care for her. The Yamaguchi Clan deserves nothing more than to be a small footnote in the history of the woman Yuki is going to be from now on – nothing more than the short comment from Tsubasa enacting punishment on them in her friend’s stead that we’ve already gotten – and any further focus on them would, in my opinion, only detract from Yuki’s redemption story rather than serve to enhance it. Her resolution should be trying to re-connect with Yumi, Akira and Tsubasa and striving to become a better person – which is *exactly* what all of the relevant post-0.50 events involving Yuki have been about – rather than taking revenge and dragging herself back into this cycle of violence and cruelty.
