CharlotteWiltshire26 said:
I also had a fairly negative reaction when I first experienced that scene – though not due to any moral/ethical considerations, but simply because it felt like it came completely out of left field and just didn’t fit with how Lessons in Love usually handles similar topics (with a hefty dose of subtlety and nuance) – yet, after ruminating on it for a couple of days and desperately trying to narratively justify the existence of “When I Say Jump” in my mind, I believe that I *did* ultimately come to understand Selebus’ intention in regards to that event and why showing Yuki’s "downfall" in full was thematically necessary and not just a meaningless “torture porn” for the sake of base-level shock value.

The general consensus at the time (and perhaps still now), if I’m not mistaken, seemed to be that both “When I Say Jump” and Yuki’s subsequent rescue by Tsubasa were a clear set-up for a future “revenge arc” of some kind where Yuki eventually returns to the Yamaguchi Clan and punishes them for what they did to her – which is why the later plot development of Tsubasa just basically solving that entire issue off-screen felt so jarring and anticlimactic to so many people, because they were expecting some great triumphant catharsis and instead got one line of dialogue. I, meanwhile, found it to be perfectly reasonable and thematically consistent, because it fell completely in-line with my personal expectations in regards to where that entire storyline is going to go:

Think back on Yuki’s entire situation prior to “When I Say Jump” and how it was as close to rock-fucking-bottom as we’ve seen for pretty much *any* character in LiL, bar none. Yuki had *literally nothing* to go on: no money (due to spending all of her already meager savings on getting drugs), no hope for the future (due to both cancer *and* her relapse, which squandered all of the progress she managed to make over the years) and no people to support her (because she intentionally tried to alienate anyone close to her and dismantle all of these personal relationships one-by-one). The only thing remaining was her completely empty and meaningless pride as “the Dragon” – something that Yuki only *says* she abandoned, despite it still clearly dictating most of her thoughts and behavior (as she herself points out to Yumi in “The Road to Recovery”: how it “feels nice” to use the Yamaguchi family name when it benefits them, but then shit-talk the yakuza and the Yamaguchi patriarch himself the very next second) – which is exactly why “When I Say Jump” was needed: to mercilessly tear down that delusional pride of hers and bring Yuki to an *actual* rock-bottom – because at that point there is nowhere else to go but *up*.

If you replay that event and pay close attention to what the narration says in regards to Yuki’s inner thoughts while she is getting raped, you’ll notice that her mindset slowly devolves from the original “do not resist, do not fight back – just persist, endure, like you’ve always done it” to a much more basic, desperate feeling of “survive, just survive, no matter the cost”:

“She wasn’t even thinking about the money anymore. She was just glad to be alive – if even for a moment longer.”

is a direct quote from the final scene of that event, clearly demonstrating how there was *nothing* inside Yuki by the point she was thrown outside into the rain – nothing except a singular deep, primal desire to *live*, reignited through pain and desperation after she already had all but completely given up on life. The woman went through a raging purifying fire and emerged victorious: abused and degraded, but unbroken, having gained a new unyielding resolve – and the World responded to that resolve by granting her a literal miracle in the form of an old friend.

In the span of mere hours, Yuki’s life turned around as rapidly as it went downhill: suddenly she was reunited with a dear figure from her long-abandoned past – a figure who, through her immense wealth and vast connections, *also* brought alongside her a possibility of salvation from a previously thought-to-be incurable affliction and an actual hope for a proper future. This is the type of shit that makes people start believing in God IRL: a clearest possible example of a “second chance” and an opportunity to start a new, better life with no prior ties or sins holding you back – so why the fuck would Yuki *ever* decide to just throw it all away and go back for the sake of “revenge” or some shit?

She has finally made a choice to stop mentally associating herself with the yakuza once and for all: no longer “Yuki the Dragon, wife of Yoshitsugu Yamaguchi” (regardless how much he hated him) but just “Yuki the person”, a thirty-something recovering addict who works in a small bar and has friends and family who care for her. The Yamaguchi Clan deserves nothing more than to be a small footnote in the history of the woman Yuki is going to be from now on – nothing more than the short comment from Tsubasa enacting punishment on them in her friend’s stead that we’ve already gotten – and any further focus on them would, in my opinion, only detract from Yuki’s redemption story rather than serve to enhance it. Her resolution should be trying to re-connect with Yumi, Akira and Tsubasa and striving to become a better person – which is *exactly* what all of the relevant post-0.50 events involving Yuki have been about – rather than taking revenge and dragging herself back into this cycle of violence and cruelty.
Click to expand...
I don't disagree with your observations as far as Yuki goes but the question my mind goes to is, "Did she need to be gangraped to illicit these feelings and this shift in mentality?" and the answer I find myself landing on is, "Nawh" lol

She was already at rock bottom going into the event as you point out yourself and being publicly torn down in front of her Yakuza peers could easily have been enough to sever that last mental connection she had with her image of being "The Dragon" and spark that desire to just be her. I won't argue that it's not thematically relevant but I don't think that in itself makes it good, I still think it was completely unnecessary to get her story and character to that point and that being publicly sexually humiliated and degraded in front of the clan was enough to justify her new character development.

I'd also add that I'm not sure that her Yakuza connection even really needed severing, personally - or re-severing, in my eyes. If it was something she'd been leaning into up until that point then sure, absolutely, but it hasn't been at all. It's not a title we even knew she held until basically immediately before that event. She's never given any indication that "Yuki the Dragon, wife of Yoshitsugu Yamaguchi" is how she views herself or that either of those things are a source of pride for her, she's always come across as someone who views herself as just a pathetic junkie and she'd already completely separated from them to take her life in a different direction before we even met her in the story.

As far as Tsubasa goes yeah, some people here did speculate there'd be a Yuki revenge storyline. I'm not one of them though lol no offence to anyone who was hoping for or thinking that but I thought it was kind of a silly idea and it would have felt super out of place to me. I just thought wrapping it up with that throwaway line was super lame lol I don't really think there needed to be any retribution or resolution there and I'd rather it was just left open than fobbed off with a lame one liner

Click to expand...
Nobody said anything about Yuki getting an automatic rifle and going back to kill the entire yakuza. Your post doesn't address what I actually said.
It isn't about the expectation of revenge, or if revenge was necessary. Revenge was taken, but it was done off-screen and communicated to the player as a "teehee" moment. If nothing had happened, fine, we'd still be waiting for it. If it was addressed and Yuki let go of it, like Tsubasa offering and she saying no - also fine, that's her decision. The way it was handled was fucking ridiculous.
Selebus chose to show the inciting event for revenge. He could very well have skipped the showing of the gangrape and skip to Yuki naked in the rain, implying it happened. But then he chooses to show it, and when it comes to the revenge he chooses not to show the revenge taking place, while communicating that it was done, as a joke? How does this equate in terms of narrative? The woman was gangraped at the lowest point of her life, does this seem funny to anyone here?

To what you actually said: If Yuki grew from it, separated herself from the past, or whatever she took out of it - great. Good for her. This isn't the point either. The point is what TheGoodPastor already replied with: "was it necessary for the scene to devolve into gangrape for this?" and I agree a 100% that it obviously didn't.

And as a last point that I didn't originally make: the whole thing doesn't even make sense. Yumi's father conceivably still wants at least a moderately civil relationship with Yumi. This destroy virtually any chance of that - his henchmen even tell him thus. Yet he thinks having his entire crew fuck his wife is a good idea for both his reputation and for his relationship with his daughter? LOL sure man, I totally buy this.

Hey, how about you also throw her naked in the street next? How about we also add some rain to the scene? And how about we add Tsubasa (that conveniently never made contact with her during all these years, despite coming in contact with Yumi several times) with a fucking umbrella and a camera angle from the defeated looking up to her?
Give me a break. Obviously Yuki's arc will take a lesson from the whole thing (one hopes at least), but you could have taken the gangrape out and it would have almost the same effect. In fact, it would be better - because it would make way more sense.

There are other ways for a character to hit rock-bottom than having her getting raped, and by choosing this Selebus invoked the harshest judgement possible on how he handles the follow-up (because it is both a very sensitive topic and overly used by bad writers), and so far I am very much not impressed.

posts.content_html_raw:
I agree with pretty much everything. I do understand that the detective was making a joke, but it is an interesting topic by itself, so I'll use it as a hook.
Anyone can be amazing in very controlled and short bursts. When you factor in that it isn't even the real world, but an entire universe that can be molded to fit what the author wants to portray, it's only really limited to a general understanding of human behavior and creativity.

All characters are Selebus, but they're also not. Even "Moonflare" isn't really me (or more than a fraction of me at least), even though it is much more myself than any of the characters in LiL are Selebus. I also highly doubt that either Rin or Maya are the people more like him, and I find it more likely that they're the people most like what he thinks of himself, portrayed in a manner that makes them look way better than the original.

I think that when you create a character what's really at play is your ability to understand human psychology. Motivations, history, limitations, struggles. And then there's the role they have in the story and their arcs. What I mean to say is that one's characters can hardly be themselves to a realistic extent. Their existence is way too limited, their role in the fictional world too specific.

Even if I create a character and say that I identify with them the most, can we really trust my judgement on it? I see multiple possible flaws there. Lastly, say that I create a character with a strong sense of retribution (which I share) - I'd heavily identify with them. Does that mean that the character is so much an extension of myself, or just an extension of a trait which isn't exclusively mine?
Tldr is you can want to fuck Rin without wanting to fuck Selebus. Once Rin is an adult though, but also maybe not because she's a fictional character. Take a look at the legislation of your own country before making a decision. This post does not incentivize any actions that would go against the law. Or common sense, in the case of Selebus.

CharlotteWiltshire26 said:
I also had a fairly negative reaction when I first experienced that scene – though not due to any moral/ethical considerations, but simply because it felt like it came completely out of left field and just didn’t fit with how Lessons in Love usually handles similar topics (with a hefty dose of subtlety and nuance) – yet, after ruminating on it for a couple of days and desperately trying to narratively justify the existence of “When I Say Jump” in my mind, I believe that I *did* ultimately come to understand Selebus’ intention in regards to that event and why showing Yuki’s "downfall" in full was thematically necessary and not just a meaningless “torture porn” for the sake of base-level shock value.

The general consensus at the time (and perhaps still now), if I’m not mistaken, seemed to be that both “When I Say Jump” and Yuki’s subsequent rescue by Tsubasa were a clear set-up for a future “revenge arc” of some kind where Yuki eventually returns to the Yamaguchi Clan and punishes them for what they did to her – which is why the later plot development of Tsubasa just basically solving that entire issue off-screen felt so jarring and anticlimactic to so many people, because they were expecting some great triumphant catharsis and instead got one line of dialogue. I, meanwhile, found it to be perfectly reasonable and thematically consistent, because it fell completely in-line with my personal expectations in regards to where that entire storyline is going to go:

Think back on Yuki’s entire situation prior to “When I Say Jump” and how it was as close to rock-fucking-bottom as we’ve seen for pretty much *any* character in LiL, bar none. Yuki had *literally nothing* to go on: no money (due to spending all of her already meager savings on getting drugs), no hope for the future (due to both cancer *and* her relapse, which squandered all of the progress she managed to make over the years) and no people to support her (because she intentionally tried to alienate anyone close to her and dismantle all of these personal relationships one-by-one). The only thing remaining was her completely empty and meaningless pride as “the Dragon” – something that Yuki only *says* she abandoned, despite it still clearly dictating most of her thoughts and behavior (as she herself points out to Yumi in “The Road to Recovery”: how it “feels nice” to use the Yamaguchi family name when it benefits them, but then shit-talk the yakuza and the Yamaguchi patriarch himself the very next second) – which is exactly why “When I Say Jump” was needed: to mercilessly tear down that delusional pride of hers and bring Yuki to an *actual* rock-bottom – because at that point there is nowhere else to go but *up*.

If you replay that event and pay close attention to what the narration says in regards to Yuki’s inner thoughts while she is getting raped, you’ll notice that her mindset slowly devolves from the original “do not resist, do not fight back – just persist, endure, like you’ve always done it” to a much more basic, desperate feeling of “survive, just survive, no matter the cost”:

“She wasn’t even thinking about the money anymore. She was just glad to be alive – if even for a moment longer.”

is a direct quote from the final scene of that event, clearly demonstrating how there was *nothing* inside Yuki by the point she was thrown outside into the rain – nothing except a singular deep, primal desire to *live*, reignited through pain and desperation after she already had all but completely given up on life. The woman went through a raging purifying fire and emerged victorious: abused and degraded, but unbroken, having gained a new unyielding resolve – and the World responded to that resolve by granting her a literal miracle in the form of an old friend.

In the span of mere hours, Yuki’s life turned around as rapidly as it went downhill: suddenly she was reunited with a dear figure from her long-abandoned past – a figure who, through her immense wealth and vast connections, *also* brought alongside her a possibility of salvation from a previously thought-to-be incurable affliction and an actual hope for a proper future. This is the type of shit that makes people start believing in God IRL: a clearest possible example of a “second chance” and an opportunity to start a new, better life with no prior ties or sins holding you back – so why the fuck would Yuki *ever* decide to just throw it all away and go back for the sake of “revenge” or some shit?

She has finally made a choice to stop mentally associating herself with the yakuza once and for all: no longer “Yuki the Dragon, wife of Yoshitsugu Yamaguchi” (regardless how much he hated him) but just “Yuki the person”, a thirty-something recovering addict who works in a small bar and has friends and family who care for her. The Yamaguchi Clan deserves nothing more than to be a small footnote in the history of the woman Yuki is going to be from now on – nothing more than the short comment from Tsubasa enacting punishment on them in her friend’s stead that we’ve already gotten – and any further focus on them would, in my opinion, only detract from Yuki’s redemption story rather than serve to enhance it. Her resolution should be trying to re-connect with Yumi, Akira and Tsubasa and striving to become a better person – which is *exactly* what all of the relevant post-0.50 events involving Yuki have been about – rather than taking revenge and dragging herself back into this cycle of violence and cruelty.

This is the type of shit that makes people start believing in God IRL: a clearest possible example of a “second chance” and an opportunity to start a new, better life with no prior ties or sins holding you back – so why the fuck would Yuki *ever* decide to just throw it all away and go back for the sake of “revenge” or some shit?

She has finally made a choice to stop mentally associating herself with the yakuza once and for all: no longer “Yuki the Dragon, wife of Yoshitsugu Yamaguchi” (regardless how much he hated him) but just “Yuki the person”, a thirty-something recovering addict who works in a small bar and has friends and family who care for her. The Yamaguchi Clan deserves nothing more than to be a small footnote in the history of the woman Yuki is going to be from now on – nothing more than the short comment from Tsubasa enacting punishment on them in her friend’s stead that we’ve already gotten – and any further focus on them would, in my opinion, only detract from Yuki’s redemption story rather than serve to enhance it. I’m on my second playthrough of The Last Sovereign. Just got to the fourth chapter. I don’t play RPG Maker games very often, but this game is one of the shining examples of how to do it right.

Sierra Lee (the dev) knocks it out of the park from every angle: characterization, storytelling and worldbuilding. Your choices actually matter too, which I definitely appreciate.

It can be tough to play an optimal run of the game, but there are luckily some good guides on the wiki to help you along.

I don’t wanna spoil too much, but if no one’s played it before and they have a lot of time on their hands, definitely give it a go.

papywavy said:
I’ve seen talk about a “green path” and a “red path” in this thread. does that mean there are two endings planned?
Click to expand...
Paraphrasing Sel, the "green path" is choosing the "correct" option every time a decision that matters is presented (or choosing to do some things before others), this path is the one that, in game terms, means you aim for 100% completion.
Meanwhile "red path", or "red paths" to be precise, is, let's say, not doing what would be expected of Sensei. In case you didn't notice, not choosing the "correct" option (or seeing an event before another sometimes) makes you miss an event (and even multiple in the future), and makes it unavailable for replay in the event list, besides changing its name and coloring it red, hence the name.
Gameplay-wise, green means you don't miss any event, and red means you missed one or more. Depending on which ones you missed, a few dialogues will change, but (for now) nothing that locks you out of advancing. My advice is to choose what you want to see, because perception is the name of the game.

In case you didn't notice, not choosing the "correct" option (or seeing an event before another sometimes) makes you miss an event (and even multiple in the future), and makes it unavailable for replay in the event list, besides changing its name and coloring it red, hence the name.
Gameplay-wise, green means you don't miss any event, and red means you missed one or more. Depending on which ones you missed, a few dialogues will change, but (for now) nothing that locks you out of advancing. My advice is to choose what you want to see, because perception is the name of the game.

Once, when I was searching something here I saw tier lists. Thought of doing mine, but didn't have any inspiration to create one. Don't want to put myself in place of MC like I just do in some other games, but what happened in event chain connected to Sensei's Quest gave me an inspiration - what if there's just one MC that like what I like. Yeah, I know, that's basically inserting myself in place of MC, but sometimes things just happens in this game, so let's pretend it's not me or I just logged in as USER 8008135.


But I wouldn't be myself, if I didn't explain why I made it like that. So, here are some explanations:

Ultimate LI:
  • Ayane - It's my favorite LI since the very beginning. Almost always passionate, positive, proactive, smart, funny and full of love towards MC. Very strong mentally to overcome obstacles and she's the first one that (reluctantly) accepted harem. She'd be my first choice for solo ending and I don't know what she'd have to do to lose this place.
Main LI:
They're LIs with whom I'd personally feel the most comfortable. No special descriptions as just listing their traits would be boring. They just seems to me like best materials for solo endings. Not 100% sure about Niki, because I'd argue with her a lot, but wholesome and too sweet life would be boring and she've proven already that there are no obstacles her love can't overcome.

Secondary LI:
They're here mostly because they're sexy or bring some traits that I'd see in harem, but I'd never consider them for solo ending.
  • Chika, Kirin, Haruka - Those three create many sexy situations. Picked them mostly for sex life, but for a long time I considered Chika much higher. She's a mix of Ayane and Ami, but for a long time I thought she took only best Ami traits, not most of them.
  • Makoto - I have mixed feelings about her. I don't really like her like most of other LIs in this group, but she'd be valuable member as she's the smartest girl from class who knows about loops and is not insane. I don't like being passive, so MC based on my traits would spend much more time searching for answers about time loops.
  • Molly - She's a gamer and my dream harem would need specialist in this category.
  • Uta, Noriko - They're just sweet and positive or act like they are.
  • Touka - Harem must have huge mansion. JK, she's here not for money purposes. She's much smarter and mature than girls her age and is a serious candidate for Main LI group, when she develop sexual traits.
Friend+sex:
That's quite original group I guess. These girls just have some traits that makes them perfect candidate for friends, but I don't really think about developing sexual relationship with them and would prefer to limit my playing time with them. I mean, I'd still fuck them, but just as a sex friend.
  • Miku - Football and running. While I don't mind watching football alone, it's not funny to play alone. Well, not really funny with only 2 people, but it's a good start to create a group. Also, running with someone else is much better and motivating than running alone.
  • Rin - For first two(?) chapters I thought she'll be Main LI, but then she changed hair started dating Otoha and I understood she's just unstable emotionally serial monogamist. That'd be ok and I would still think about her as a Secondary LI, but then I met Rika and imagined older Rin as someone very similar to her. Rin is smarter than Rika, so she still would be a great friend, but not someone that MC with my traits would spend too much time.
  • Yuki - Badass friend and great drinking companion. Much different life experience than everybody else.
  • Wakana - Best friend material. She's not Secondary LI only because I wouldn't want to destroy what she has with Osako. That says a lot about how I respect her character as I'm netori fan.
  • Osako - If/when they break with Wakana, she's being automatically dropped to Unattractive. I'd want her to be kept close as a friend, but mostly because there'd be a possibility of threesome and would want MC to be considered as a sperm donor, if they decide to have a child with Wakana.
Mixed feelings:
  • Yumi, IO - I like them and I want to help them. But I don't see them as a part of the group, because of their attitude, nor in sexual context.
  • Maya - She have too many negative traits, with thousand years of experience and just after reset. She's just a bitch... but I guess that she's the key.
  • Chinami - I just want her to feel happy and safe.
Unattractive:
I wouldn't feel any different, if they just get removed from the game and their roles get replaced by someone. Some of them are just tokens and others may have some story impact, but don't bring any emotions in me.

Untrusted:
  • Ami - Crazy psycho.
  • Yasu - On one hand she also may be they key like Maya, but on another she may just have schizophrenia. But how she knows so many things? I don't trust her in this point of the game.
  • Kaori - She jumped from Unattractive to Untrusted after events on the roof before Sensei's Quest.
  • Tsubasa - Too manipulative with too big power. If she gets bored, she may do too big harm.
  • Nao - Yeah... what's going on with her? Is she even real?

Moonflare said:
Either Maya was granted to Akira 1, or we never saw Akira 1. Following the rules of "a wish is granted to a you that never made it", Maya would have been granted to Akira 2 (after Akira 1 wished for her - and never got her).

Then, Akira 2 died (we assume), and Maya made a wish to create a world for him. And this turned into a whole thing because she herself got into her world. This I think is less lore-breaking because she shouldn't be able to make a wish in the first place. So she being able to enter her own wish is okay in comparison.

But yes, eventually her Akira (Akira 2) enters 23, as the game begins (our Akira). Which is the same Akira that eventually leaves 23 and has Himawari. This is the main theory.

Other theories could be that our Akira could be Akira 1, and he never met Maya (thus the lack of memories about her). Or Maya Prime could be Maya 2, also a being created by original Maya's wish. Maybe actual Maya is shadow Maya, that shows up in "Frankincense" - and she's watching it all play out as a powerless observer. Lots of theories.
Click to expand...
Disclaimer: This is based off memory, so I may be misremembering what Himawari actually said.
Considering Himawari's mention of wanting everyone to just wish for a new flavor of Kit Kat, it seems unlikely that every wish creates a new world and a new person who gets to enjoy that wish while the wisher doesn't. (Making new worlds for every new Kit Kat wouldn't change the problem)

Wishes that just add things to a world's present, probably don't create a new world, and presumably are given to the wisher. This seems to be what Maya and Nao-chan are. Just things added to a world. No past necessary.

However, wishes that alter reality, like changing the past, or ensuring a future, etc, likely create new worlds.

Basically what time travel would do in theory. Instead of changing the time traveler's world (which should make it so that they shouldn't exist in the first place to do this), a new world with that altered timeline is created, while the old world remains unchanged.

The Kit Kat scenario is comparable to just feeding a fish in a bowl, with the wisher being the fish, and the feed coming from outside the bowl.
---

In theory: Maya's wish involved the real Akira and real Maya in a way that would make it impossible not to include them in her wish world in a certain way, which might be causing things to become convoluted.

I also wouldn't be surprised if her wish created an eternal romantic tragedy that would constantly lead to them falling in love again and again no matter what the world throws at them. Which might have also made the world sentient and established it's hatred for Maya, since it's created just to ultimately fail no matter what.

Like Maya has said:
(Chapter 4 'Sweet Joy Befall Thee! Be Nice to Sensei Battle!' Main Event)
Frankly, I wouldn't be surprised to find out that Himawari is just another example of what the world is throwing at them.

Or there's just some other convoluted reason for these things. Sel seems to hint at multiple wishes leading to this world, so Maya's might just be at the center. (Albeit, technically it's Sensei's wish's wish, but who knows, Sensei might be a wish's wish as well. It did apparently start before he was born.)

Maybe Yuu's wish to make his harem happy created this multiverse to start with.

posts.content_html_raw:
john doeer said:
I'd say thats one of my biggest open questions. How is it possible that both Maya and Himawari can sincerely claim he is "their" Akira? Ostensibly its Akira 1 wish creating Maya for Akira 2, leaving Akira 1 to elope with Ayane. However, both of them believe its their flesh and blood OG Akira. Is it a timey whimey excuse or something more concrete? Nodoka has remarked on him "slipping" physically between worlds so maybe he did something like that unknowingly. Beyond that all I have is many rolls of tin foil.
Click to expand...
There's no guarantee that Akira wishing for Maya created a new world, but the wishes that create new worlds create copies of people to inhabit them, which is what Maya's wish did.

The start of the game implies this Akira was in the dark for a while and whoever's narrating the passage is moving them after finding them discarded for a long time, unsure if it's because the old world died or whatever happened was cataclysmic enough for Maya to specifically wish for a new world, presumably after witnessing something wiping Akira's memories like Scary Room implies.

As for this Maya entering the world she created, we don't know for certain but there's been plenty of allegories and theories about Maya having wings / being a bird who can cross between worlds. Birds might be a funamental thing about the wishing well, Ayane claimed in the last update that she starts hearing birds whenever she thinks about the memories she has lost, there might be a connection between the two. Considering all the other weird shit like her love being so strong that she was able to wish for a world as a wish, I'm not putting it off the table until the game supplies a better explanation.

Himawari is pretty easy, she knows more about how these worlds work than any of us. She'd have the tools to figure it out, including finding her Akira who might have been lost in the worlds that have been shut down, or knowing where everyone in those worlds ends up, maybe at the bottom of the well.

posts.content_html_raw:
Have we discussed how large Kumon-Mi is as a city/district? Is there farmland within the city limits? If not, do they use vertical greenhouses? What about meat? We know that yes, restaurants have access to live chickens, but what about beef? There's an ocean still which means fish is an acceptable food (though is there just a giant wall out in the sea, almost like the Truman Show?)

How do supply chains even work? Where are they getting the raw material from, and how large is the industrial area there? Surely there must be an immense amount of plastic available for the two bubble wrap families (though is post still possible with the wall?)

All in all, Sel's world building seems a little shaky and I'm worried about his competency as an author.

I need an update. Once a month is tooooo looooooong.

SlidingSubject said:
Now I wonder, if LiL was something mainstream, how would an actually "isekai'd into Sensei" thing go so it could be long-term instead of a one-shot where Ami kills you for not being her Sensei? Would someone without Sensei's traumas and triggers be able to survive, and maybe thrive, while being in his place on Kumon-mi?
Click to expand...
DeanNoriko said:
But nobody other than Akira would be considered "Sensei" at all. It's not really an isekai, even though the game makes you think it is in the beginning. That's the thing, Maya, Ami, Himawari etc. consider the "real" Sensei real based on the fact that he remembers being Akira.

That being said, if somebody did get isekai'd into that world into Akira's body, somehow, then I think it would go unnoticed for quite a while, almost no matter what you do, since Maya (and probably Ami too) has experienced millions of versions of Sensei that all differed and had their own characteristics, like the football fanatic Sensei that only ever really fucked with Karin of all people. He seemed quite tame all things considered, compared to actual Akira.
Click to expand...
Frankly, after Himawari's wish-world seemed to add memories to our Ayane and Sensei, basically brainwashing them into Himawari's idea of perfect parents:
(Chapter 4 Ayane 'Bitter Cherries' Event)

It seems like that may be the fate of anyone isekai'd into someone in a wish-world.

Whether or not someone actually is Sensei, being in his body might just rewrite them into Sensei eventually, and with everyone just going along with his amnesia, things probably won't be much different than they were in Chapter 1. Although, assuming the isekai'd person recalls their own life before it's rewritten, they'd surely be more driven to either enjoy or escape things.

Overall: Even our Sensei could just be becoming the "real" Sensei because that might be how the world works.

Not to mention, there's always the possibility that the Isekai'd person would just be reset a few months in, if that. Or have someone/thing "slip" into their body and take over.

This world is pretty horrifying if you think about it. Maya Prime was very used to Sensei just changing personalities:
(Chapter 1 'Tradition' Main Event)

It also seems unlikely that besides Ayane, Maya, and potentially the Nakayamas, the rest of the girls would notice or care, as long as it's his body, and he still wants to fuck them.

Ami in particular doesn't seem to think our Sensei is the "real" one. At one point, considering him a "half-eaten replica":
(Chapter 4 Ami 'Della' Event)
And Ami Prime doesn't seem to find him all that special compared to other Senseis that she's surely known, either.

Dude has moved away to Korea, and gets called back after 9 years because his sister is at the hospital, and for some god-forsaken reason they have to read him her will ???? (she's alive wtf).

Then her will says that she's making him inherit a teacher position ?????????????? (it's not even that she owns the school, she's literally just a teacher)

The whole time her daughters are demeaning you, telling you to go back to Korea, that you can't call her mom because she didn't birth you (even though she raised you) and get this: the lawyer says he's not allowed to let you read the will yourself WHAT and that if you refuse to take your part of the inheritance (20% of the shares that you can't even manage), the other heirs will get higher taxes and receive less (WHAT)

It's just nonsense after nonsense. I can't even.

posts.content_html_raw:
Stream of consciousness time for that other game.
Asuna in the main menu. Seems like a regular call. Ah, yes, the usual nonsensical rambles, but it feels like it's a bit more... trite than the others? the piano is a good touch tho. Blatant wallbreak so soon? I recognize that bridge! This entire sequence man, it's too much. I feel like giving up but I'll make it to the end. Well, at least he doesn't look like Sensei. The entire office scene somehow felt more boring than the coffee segment. Ohh, this isn't a song I heard, but for a second it reminded me of a Dissonance song. The regular train section felt wholly unnecesary except for that one thing. The dark train section feels like dream logic. No, wait, still conscious, more like a LiL happy event, but why so soon? Okay, it's an animation, but why the camera movement? Speaking in a meta way, LiL has the protagonist at the center of an anomaly though not as the originator of it, [redacted] has this guy who partitioned his own segment of reality to try and rule, with the protagonist being a variant who got slided from his mundane world to a new one. Dissonance, though still not really finished but a bit more advanced, implies the protagonist may be the overseer of that reality. Sorrow of Rebirth has the guy being an unwitting pawn for others. The sex talk makes me think this game is a bit more aligned with Dissonance in that meta way. Lol, I saw that hair movement fail. So that's one niece, at least one normal conversation here. That's the other niece. Both have the same smile, but one isn't supposed to be smiling, not even smirking. Oh, a few image changes and it's a correct expression. I just remembered that I hate how 5heads are the default in KK and you have to make good shots to conceal or gloss over it, not that it's that bad just noticeable sometimes. Is there some "only a few open mouth images per scene" tax? I think the music should've started after they entered the building, felt a bit dissonant hearing peppy-ish tunes while reading about death. I remember the LiL jokes about americanisms and how they're actually japanese. Oh, so this is the in to how he gets roped into the town by the lawyer. That's the first decision that doesn't matter (jump one doesn't count).

Okay, I can't anymore. I tried, really, but this is where I fall. I'll check its thread in 5 updates just to see if it can be something good. Because until now it feels like an even weirder mix of contrivances than any of the games I've mentioned.
EDIT: Can I say how it's funny that technically, besides LiL, the other games are more LiL inspired rather than outright clones? Sure, some story vibes may look similar, but they are their own thing.

Moonflare said:
Dude has moved away to Korea, and gets called back after 9 years because his sister is at the hospital, and for some god-forsaken reason they have to read him her will ???? (she's alive wtf).

Then her will says that she's making him inherit a teacher position ?????????????? (it's not even that she owns the school, she's literally just a teacher)
Click to expand...
Okay, now that I'm actually playing this and not just reading commentary -- it's a will SIGNING, not a will READING. Will signing very much requires the estate owner to still be alive. Can't sign when you're dead and all that. And witnesses are required to be present in some jurisdictions.

And if a responsibility is being passed down, the person receiving the responsibility would likely need to be there to consent to taking on that burden -- in theory, this would ideally be done well in advance, but in emergent situations this doesn't seem all that unusual. The most unusual thing about this from where I am in the game so far is that this is being done on an emergent basis. If it's a particularly large estate or includes a major responsiblity being passed over, this should have been sorted out and locked in well before someone is on their deathbed.

I'm only on the phone call right now, so I may be missing something, and I absolutely agree with the "this feels derivative to the point of laziness" up to this point.

Edit: ...and now he's in town and they're calling it a reading. Ugh. I think this really was written by AI.

posts.content_html_raw:
Hello. A couple of months ago, after going through version 0.51 and thinking it over a bit, I decided to replay Lil during my two-week break (yes, yes — I knew from the start how ridiculous that would be), while keeping an “archive” of metaphors, quotes, and simply pleasant moments.
Now I’m at the events of version 0.31 and I’ve simply given up trying to endure this feeling of despair from not understanding the metaphors and their repetitions — the number of which is growing to an incomparably large extent. On the first playthrough I could easily suppress these feelings and surrender to the moment, since I didn’t have to keep an archive; but now it just eats at me, and a huge amount of my NOT-free time that I devote to maintaining my dependence on this story is spent on pathetic escapism. (The run up to 0.31 took 168 hours of playtime, and I don’t know how many of those I was actually playing. The archive doesn’t take that much time.)

Could you recommend any books, lectures, or other reading to help me understand it better?
(I feel like I'm in a spoiler-minefield right now.)

Hello. A couple of months ago, after going through version 0.51 and thinking it over a bit, I decided to replay Lil during my two-week break (yes, yes — I knew from the start how ridiculous that would be), while keeping an “archive” of metaphors, quotes, and simply pleasant moments.
Now I’m at the events of version 0.31 and I’ve simply given up trying to endure this feeling of despair from not understanding the metaphors and their repetitions — the number of which is growing to an incomparably large extent. On the first playthrough I could easily suppress these feelings and surrender to the moment, since I didn’t have to keep an archive; but now it just eats at me, and a huge amount of my NOT-free time that I devote to maintaining my dependence on this story is spent on pathetic escapism. (The run up to 0.31 took 168 hours of playtime, and I don’t know how many of those I was actually playing. The archive doesn’t take that much time.)

Could you recommend any books, lectures, or other reading to help me understand it better?
(I feel like I'm in a spoiler-minefield right now.)
View attachment 5654795
Click to expand...
A fellow “archive-keeper”, huh? Tip of the hat to you, genuinely. It’s nice to see that I’m not alone in my relentless obsession with keeping notes and documenting anything and everything that piques my interest – which in this particular case happens to be *a whole lot* (and is also borderline a necessity when it comes to trying to understand some of the more esoteric aspects of LiL’s narrative).

Still, just to clarify: what *exactly* are you seeking help with here? Because learning the intricacies of abstract media analysis and the methodology of properly interpreting symbolism pretty much from scratch is… not really something that can be done by simply reading a textbook or two or watching a handy YouTube tutorial, I’m afraid – and even if you *could* do such a thing, considering that we’re speaking about something as dense and incomprehensible as this eldritch fucking abomination, I’m not sure how much it would *actually* help you in practice, because Selebus’ writing can frequently be both extremely flowery and cryptic as fuck, and Lessons in Love as a whole is literally the farthest thing from being a beginner-level text.

With that being said, however, discussing some specific examples of repeating metaphors that you particularly struggle to comprehend the meaning of *is* very much possible – and, with some luck, it could even give you an idea of how to approach all of the other similar cases (by applying the same thought process to them, as well). So if that is something that you would be interested in, feel free to ask further questions – just with a bit more specificity this time around.

Ughhh, I feel like a rubber ball that crumbles the moment you touch it.

I've been having trouble for a long time understanding the event’s narrative.
I think it started with “Somewhere Far From Here”, when Yasu 73756464656e decided to combine a Bus driving backwards, 357 mirrors, the sounds of the Ocean and the question «Why do we hurt?».
At first I had no problem taking in those metaphors, but with each new mention I get more and more confused, and my broken brain only makes things worse.
The worst part is when you spend a long time thinking about some narrative or some metaphor, and the next day you can't formulate a single word about it, while the feeling that those thoughts really happened and led somewhere sits too firmly in your head and annoys you. (Stairs/steps in the bar; a Bus driving backwards; Light, Darkness and the parking Mike’s santa present; Shoreline Yumi/Noriko/Plants; the motif of Reflection.)

Right now, while playing through it, I just stumble over these basic motifs such as Summer, Heat and Nudity; Winter, Cold and Scarf; insectual and bird omens; world’s edge/top, Moon and ability to fly/jump. The last trio is the hardest to understand so far.
And it's too difficult for me to ask you to explain such simple(??) things, so I wanted to know what literature those who understand at least something might recommend — not necessarily useful.
(Probably because you’ve been steeped in this noodle-soup for years.)

(While trying to re-examine the events on the beach, I bumped into two disputed points:
Did Noriko even exist in the first years of Sensei and Niki's relationship?
What is the black sphere that Sensei is looking at in norikopresent16?)

But I decided to ask for help after going through “Where the Trees Live.” Let’s put it this way: I understood absolutely nothing. Specifically:
- At what points does Sensei start counting the streetlights?
- The twice-repeated phrase about the Moon that haunts the car.

Does this tell us anything about Kaori’s awareness? Awareness of what?

THaT SOmetHIng nEVer FEelS RIgHT!
The sting of death has robbed me of my only given life.
These spare parts move my body, yet shift nothing found outside.
Every time I feel a thought rush in, it's maimed and left behind.
Now I cannot help but wonder why I lived and never died.
Every day I grow some more.

It would be useful to read an explanation of what the Creaking of the Stairs means (and, apparently, the staircase as a whole), as mentioned in:

Thank you for your promptness, but as you can see, I can't keep up with it.

Edited.
Most delightful.
Sensei's monologue at the beginning of "Worry Not, The Mason Jar" (which comes right after the kiss with Kaori in "Run, Rabbit, Run") is a new high point in my incomprehension of Sensei's words.

I would be very grateful for an analysis of this text (or at least for an indication of the approximate dates when it was discussed among these 60k messages).

spoilers.title: Something
spoilers.html:
I think it started with “Somewhere Far From Here”, when Yasu 73756464656e decided to combine a Bus driving backwards, 357 mirrors, the sounds of the Ocean and the question «Why do we hurt?».
At first I had no problem taking in those metaphors, but with each new mention I get more and more confused, and my broken brain only makes things worse.
The worst part is when you spend a long time thinking about some narrative or some metaphor, and the next day you can't formulate a single word about it, while the feeling that those thoughts really happened and led somewhere sits too firmly in your head and annoys you. (Stairs/steps in the bar; a Bus driving backwards; Light, Darkness and the parking Mike’s santa present; Shoreline Yumi/Noriko/Plants; the motif of Reflection.)

Right now, while playing through it, I just stumble over these basic motifs such as Summer, Heat and Nudity; Winter, Cold and Scarf; insectual and bird omens; world’s edge/top, Moon and ability to fly/jump. The last trio is the hardest to understand so far.
And it's too difficult for me to ask you to explain such simple(??) things, so I wanted to know what literature those who understand at least something might recommend — not necessarily useful.
(Probably because you’ve been steeped in this noodle-soup for years.)

(While trying to re-examine the events on the beach, I bumped into two disputed points:
Did Noriko even exist in the first years of Sensei and Niki's relationship?
What is the black sphere that Sensei is looking at in norikopresent16?)

Lessons in Love might just be the greatest romance I’ve ever read.

this dev is a demon who can manipulate my feelings at will, and I can’t tell whether I like it or hate it. maybe both.

I knew Sel was evil and was going to take it all away.
The dude straight up baited me with multiple possible subplots in Aomori T-T

Some of the things you mention I'd need to replay through scenes to jog my memory, but I'll walk through the ones I can help with right away. There may be spoilers, I don't know how far into the game you are, and one of my biggest problems with this game is that there is so much of it the order of scenes gets jumbled in my brain.

Whenever Sensei mentions a car, it's safe to assume it's a reference to the car accident that killed his sister-in-law/lover/abuser. That event is life-defining event upon which most of the game revolves. The moon haunting the car just means the he associates the moon with the accident as well.

The first of the images I quoted from your post is actually a recurring image, but the girl on the right changes the other time it's used. Here, it's Kaori. The other time, it's Sensei's dead lover wearing the same dress. These scenes happen pretty close to each other, IIRC, very likely in the same update.

The History image hints that Kaori is aware of Sensei's predatory nature, and this poem hints at why. I'll bold the relevant bit

THaT SOmetHIng nEVer FEelS RIgHT!
The sting of death has robbed me of my only given life.
These spare parts move my body, yet shift nothing found outside.
Every time I feel a thought rush in, it's maimed and left behind.
Now I cannot help but wonder why I lived and never died.
Every day I grow some more.

Kaori has a scar on her abdomen. Yumi mentions that her cousin (Kaori) was in a really bad accident, and that she had thought Kaori dead for years. "spare parts" implies that Kaori survived because of a transplant, and it's very possible that "every day I grow some more" is indicating that the person who's body provided the organ(s) is slowly taking over or exerting more influence over Kaori.

When you put the repeated image, the repeated motif of a car accident, and the organ transplant together, it becomes "Kaori survived because Sekai was an organ donor" and a piece of Sekai's conciousness is growing inside her.

Moving on to stairs.

My takeaway is that the seventh stair is just a memory or emotion you avoid making contact with, a piece of trauma you refuse to unpack and deal with, that just continues rotting away at you until you're forced to deal with it -- by which time it can often be too late.

Sara's Seventh Stair is her dead son. She refuses to talk about him, changes the subject immediately when he's brought up, and refuses to let herself heal. It isn't until she realizes that Sana's beginning to pull away from her that she finally even acknowledges that he ever existed. Sensei knows he existed because Sana talks about him openly when Sara isn't around, but he never brings him up. Whenever he navigates the staircase, he makes sure to step around the subject. But eventually, the wood around the seventh step begins to rot as well, and Sana will have to deal with the consequences of that neglect at some point.

Okay, so, I’ll try to give helpful explanations – or at the very least a few widely accepted theories/interpretations – wherever I can, but apologies in advance if I’ve accidentally misunderstood the specifics of what confuses you the most: your comment is pretty big and reads somewhat like an unfocused stream of consciousness (not a criticism; just an impartial observation), so I’m, admittedly, having some trouble properly parsing all of it in my head.

A lot of metaphors and thematic elements that you mention in your “Something” part (like summer and winter, light and darkness, sun and moon, allusions to insects and other living creatures, etcetera) are directly related to the Trinity: HOPE, Tenchou and Pareidolia, the three main Gods presiding over Kumon-mi – so if you struggle to properly comprehend the full deeper meaning behind those symbols, I would suggest first trying to understand the individual symbology of each of those three: what are their main elements/attributes, what “divine” aspects they embody, which familiars/servants they use to indirectly carry out their will and other things along those lines. Luckly for you, about a month ago I wrote two very extensive posts about this very subject (№61604 and №61608, I believe), so you can look for them and find all of the relevant information there.

Aside from that:

– The “bus riding backwards”, the Hall of Mirrors and the ocean are all barely understood mysteries that we still don’t really have concrete answers for. The bus appears to be vaguely connected to the general motif of “things being backwards” (exemplified by “Arms Bent Back”, “Backwards Dancing”, “Backwards Boulevard” and other similar events/mentions), in addition to just generally being Sensei’s most frequently used transportation choice when he has to travel long distances across town, thus somewhat symbolizing “movement” or “progress”; the mirror thing is linked with both Amiokay (she is the same “mirror girl” that was mentioned by Yasu, judging by the Japanese text-to-speech in “Rain King”) and Pareidolia (who is seemingly the one narrating in Futaba’s “Hall of Mirrors”), in addition to also being mentioned in Yumi’s TSS, I believe; and, finally, the ocean is just overall something very important to the “meta” aspect of the narrative, judging by the constant references to it (like in “Wings of Anhedonia”) and the entire Transpacific Sadness Symposium event line.

– “Why do things have to hurt so much?” (or some other similar variation) is a question that gets repeatedly brought up by various characters throughout the entire story simply because it is directly relevant to one of main themes of Lessons in Love: trying to deal with trauma or otherwise significantly painful life events. It’s one of the game’s many, many thesis statements – nothing more, nothing less.

– The bird metaphors don’t really have a single unifying element, as far as I’m aware, and mostly stem from the specifics of characters/situations of when they are introduced, in addition to being fairly unambiguous and self-evident: the marsh warbler motif is directly related to Akira (how he constantly imitates others and pretends to be someone he’s not: an adult, a teacher, a parent and a “normal human” – as part of his “hunting/survival” strategy), Maya is connected to magpies through the legend of Altair and Vega (which is mentioned in her “Everlasting Mercy” event and is basically a one-to-one match with Maya’s and Akira’s own current situation), and Nodoka is associated with a white-fronted parrot due to the specifics of their mating behavior (because it is *also* a one-to-one match with Akira’s and Nodoka’s relationship and what he metaphorically/thematically does to her in “White-Fronted Parrot”).

– “Top of the world” is the school rooftop, which is repeatedly mentioned as being the highest point in the entire city multiple times in Chapter 1. “The edge of the world” could also refer to the roof, or the beach (as it is directly connected to the ocean), or some other not-yet-revealed meta-location. Sensei's monologue at the beginning of "Worry Not, The Mason Jar" (which comes right after the kiss with Kaori in "Run, Rabbit, Run") is a new high point in my incomprehension of Sensei's words.

I would be very grateful for an analysis of this text (or at least for an indication of the approximate dates when it was discussed among these 60k messages).
Click to expand...
Oh, also: sorry for double-posting, but after re-reading “Worry Not, The Mason Jar” and thinking about it for a while, I believe that I now have a much better idea of what Sensei (and, by extension, Selebus) was trying to convey through that – admittedly, really fucking cryptic – monologue.

It’s important to note the *exact point* in which “Worry Not, The Mason Jar” is placed within LiL’s grand overarching narrative: it happens relatively early into the second half of Chapter 3 (specifically, version 0.31), which is shortly preceded by those three incredibly important Niki events where Akira finally remembers his name (version 0.29) and is followed fairly soon after by the fourth Halloween (version 0.35), where Akira truly believes that he is going to get Reset (due to “not taking something that did not belong to him” like he was repeatedly instructed).

So, to reiterate: this event is placed directly in-between Sensei finally coming to terms with being an actual person with an actual past (the past that now actively *haunts* him in the form of Sekaori, as seen during “Run, Rabbit, Run (Why the Fieldmice Hide)”, the literal previous event) *and* him starting to seriously contemplate the concept of “mortality” (not literal mortality, but a metaphorical one – as in, the idea of him being replaced by a “different” Sensei) due to what happened with Maya earlier during the fourth Reset in addition to him actively and continually disobeying the will of a higher power. It’s clear that Akira has been subtly plagued by fear and uncertainty of what is going to happen to him in the future for quite a while now, which prompts this particular bout of self-reflection, with him trying to come to terms with his irreversibly changing current situation. When looking at it from that perspective, a lot of previously incomprehensible lines he says in “Worry Not, The Mason Jar” suddenly begin to make a lot more sense.

He begins by talking directly to “you” – the mysterious entity that constantly observes all of his actions (something that Sensei is perfectly aware of and occasionally mentions in his narration, like at the end of Maya’s “Anything & Everything”, for example) – and making a deliberate distinction between himself as he actually is and himself how “you” perceive him (“reflected through this jar I’m trapped inside”). Akira follows it up by bringing up the idea of “change” (initially in the form of simply growing up) that at first seems completely unrelated to anything he was saying earlier, but is then symbolically connected to his previous lines through the aforementioned jar metaphor:

“My hands grace the glass of my infinite jar, staring back at someone I can only view as the protagonist of this story, while the only thing that *truly* matters is the glass itself. It that shatters, what comes next? How will the creature (me) inside of it (the jar) appear to the untrained eye when filled with shards of my former home […]? For even if my breathing were to continue after such a tragic event, I’d not be seen as who I *am* but who I *was*.”

I can come up with two equally likely ways to interpret this metaphor, both of which have to do with the same exact subject of *perception*:

The first interpretation leans into the idea that by learning more and more about his past he gradually stops being “Sensei” (the nameless, formless nobody who reincarnated into someone else’s body) and becomes “Akira” (an actual person who existed; who belongs here) – and it fucking terrifies him. The “jar” is the façade that he was wearing all this time: a façade of an uncaring, cool and mysterious dude could afford to not give a shit about anything by the virtue of “well, this isn’t my world, so I don’t have to care” – but now it *is* his world and he *does* have to care, and so Akira wonders what will happen to his carefully cultivated public persona when he is forced to actually acknowledge his past and properly deal with its consequences, rather then simply saying “it doesn’t matter” whenever he finds it too inconvenient.

The second interpretation is a lot more charitable to Akira and leans much more into the introspective/philosophical side compared to the first one, though they still ultimately stem from the very same source. His line “for even if my breathing were to continue after such a tragic event, I’d not be seen as who I *am* but who I *was*” can also be taken not as fearful apprehension of a callous coward, but rather as pessimistic musings of someone who was lucky enough to not be chained down by his past (due to literally being reborn in a new world as a new person, with nothing holding him back) and is now realizing that this past has finally caught up to him. He can no longer just be “Sensei” (a blank slate with no prior sins or personal baggage, free to be whoever he wants) and is instead forced to take up the mantle of “Akira” (a very specific “someone” with an *unimaginable* amount of personal baggage). As of right now, there is still a decent level of separation between the two – the metaphorical “glass of the infinite jar” – and thus he still has *some* wiggle room, but once enough “shards of my former home” are put inside the jar and the glass inevitably shatters, everyone is *only* going to see him as Akira – an incredibly broken and deeply traumatized person – rather than his current self as Sensei: the man he *wants* to be perceived as.

Either way, the monologue ends with Sensei once again suppressing these thoughts and sealing them in the farthest confines of his mind, because running from personal issues through escapism and willful ignorance is Akira’s №1 way of doing things. Thus, he tries to convince both “you” *and* himself that “I lied: everything *has* been looking up” and that “there is nothing for me to fix, since the world is going to fix it for me”, concluding it all on a very telling “warble, warble, warble” line, signifying that the time for self-reflection is over and that he is now fully back in his usual “mimicry” mode.

The first interpretation leans into the idea that by learning more and more about his past he gradually stops being “Sensei” (the nameless, formless nobody who reincarnated into someone else’s body) and becomes “Akira” (an actual person who existed; who belongs here) – and it fucking terrifies him. The “jar” is the façade that he was wearing all this time: a façade of an uncaring, cool and mysterious dude could afford to not give a shit about anything by the virtue of “well, this isn’t my world, so I don’t have to care” – but now it *is* his world and he *does* have to care, and so Akira wonders what will happen to his carefully cultivated public persona when he is forced to actually acknowledge his past and properly deal with its consequences, rather then simply saying “it doesn’t matter” whenever he finds it too inconvenient.
The second interpretation is a lot more charitable to Akira and leans much more into the introspective/philosophical side compared to the first one, though they still ultimately stem from the very same source. His line “for even if my breathing were to continue after such a tragic event, I’d not be seen as who I *am* but who I *was*” can also be taken not as fearful apprehension of a callous coward, but rather as pessimistic musings of someone who was lucky enough to not be chained down by his past (due to literally being reborn in a new world as a new person, with nothing holding him back) and is now realizing that this past has finally caught up to him. He can no longer just be “Sensei” (a blank slate with no prior sins or personal baggage, free to be whoever he wants) and is instead forced to take up the mantle of “Akira” (a very specific “someone” with an *unimaginable* amount of personal baggage). As of right now, there is still a decent level of separation between the two – the metaphorical “glass of the infinite jar” – and thus he still has *some* wiggle room, but once enough “shards of my former home” are put inside the jar and the glass inevitably shatters, everyone is *only* going to see him as Akira – an incredibly broken and deeply traumatized person – rather than his current self as Sensei: the man he *wants* to be perceived as.
Either way, the monologue ends with Sensei once again suppressing these thoughts and sealing them in the farthest confines of his mind, because running from personal issues through escapism and willful ignorance is Akira’s №1 way of doing things. Thus, he tries to convince both “you” *and* himself that “I lied: everything *has* been looking up” and that “there is nothing for me to fix, since the world is going to fix it for me”, concluding it all on a very telling “warble, warble, warble” line, signifying that the time for self-reflection is over and that he is now fully back in his usual “mimicry” mode.

Click to expand...
Yeah, basically. There isn't a call involved though.

You can do up to Chika's event 'A dog that doesn't do math', the event in the shopping mall where Sensei and Chinami (in her dog mask) bump into Maya and Ami. After that is her event 'Shaudenfreude', which is the event in which Sensei fingers Chika and is interrupted by Makoto and it's triggered by visiting Chika's dorm room. This event you have to wait until after the beach trip event chain to do if you want to be a "good homie" and see all of Rin's events. This is one of two extremely easy to fall into pitfalls for a first playthrough.

The second pitfall I alluded to also involves Chika, but it's a bit easier to see coming. In chapter two she will mention winning some tickets to a hot springs and you'll be told you can trigger the event by calling her on a Saturday - the game will warn you to talk to Yumi first but you actually need to do several events with Yumi if you don't want to miss anything.

Specifically you need to watch up to (and including) Yumi's event 'Abyss' before making that call.

It's not a terribly bad thing to have messed up here, mind you. You do miss a couple of Rin's events as a result but her dialogue throughout the first three chapters of the game is altered quite substantially as she frequently makes jokes and snide remarks about Sensei's betrayal so it's quite an interesting change.

That being said it's probably a better thing to do intentionally for a subsequent playthrough so you can compare and contrast so yeah, if it's not too much hassle going back and course correcting might be for the best.

As always I'll recommend you download the guide mod on the first page - it will tell you which events you have available, what their pre-requisites are if you don't already meet them and most importantly it will tell you in a non-spoilery way what choices you need to make in order to avoid missing content. It can become quite a chore later in the game to progress without the guide mod.

Hello friends. I've had a busy month and missed out on the initial 0.55 discussion, but there's something I'd still like to talk about: the newest hints about Rin's biological family. Onund asked her about her bio mom, revealing some things in the process:
I could be wrong, but I think he's also talking about Rin's secret sister in this passage. I'm going to start the discussion there.
The Rokuharas have said that Rin's dad was a "huge cheat" and may have had another family. It's fairly likely that he had other children and that someone found out about it - otherwise how would the Rokuharas know?

With that in mind, it makes a lot of sense to me that Onund's phrase "another you" refers to a half-sister of Rin. Finding out that such a person exists would be a big deal to Rin's mom, because it would also mean finding out that her "partner" isn't just unfaithful, he's been hiding a whole second family. That kind of shock could cause her to "leave" (more on this in the next section).

For those that don't know, I (and many others) believe that Rin and Sana are half-sisters. Sana is also a perfect fit for the other clues that Onund gives:
  • She's smaller than Rin.
  • She's more broken than Rin. (Understatement of the year)
  • There's something special about her that the gods want.
  • Gods who are more important than Onund have been trying to secure her favor.
Pegasus has made multiple attempts to get her to give herself to him, similar to what Onund does with Rin in her TSS. Pegasus is supposedly a Peerless One, making him important in the hierarchy of gods (although I have doubts about his legitimacy).



It's not just Pegasus; Sana said other gods have been doing the same thing, and Sekaori/USER3 seem very interested in getting her to accept any god at all.




Sana has something they want, something that's probably intrinsic to her since her mother went through the same thing when she was younger.

The only other character I can think of to fit these clues is Ami, but we haven't seen direct evidence of gods trying to gain her favor like with Sana. Add that to all of the preexisting hints of Sana's connection to Rin, and it's far more likely to be her.
The claim that Rin's bio mom "left" is interesting, because from what we know she never physically went anywhere, certainly not by choice. She was forced to give Rin up for adoption because her mental issues made her unable to raise a child on her own, and it's implied (or possibly outright stated, I don't remember) that she was institutionalized somewhere.

There's another possible meaning, though: she left mentally, in much the same way that Sensei's mind can slip to other worlds during his blackouts. While Sensei always returns from his mental slips, we know that it's possible for a slip to be one-way, for someone's mind to get stuck somewhere else - something like that happened to Kyoko Nagasawa. And there's a similarity in how Rin's mom "could barely speak" and how Kyoko is unable to respond to Nodoka.

Sensei's blackouts are often triggered by mental distress, when some aspect of his trauma gets dredged up. I'm guessing the shock of finding out that Rin's dad had a second family served as a similar trigger for Rin's mom, causing her mind to retreat from the situation.


A couple questions occur to me based on the above hints. These are very speculative and probably don't go anywhere, but they're worth thinking about.

1. If Rin's mom found out about Sara's family, did Sara find out about Rin's mom?
A long time ago Sara said that someone eventually found out about her relationship with her teacher, but we've never learned who that was or what the consequences were. Maybe it was Rin's mom. Sara did also say that she never knew who any of her teacher's other girls were, which would seem to preclude that, but after her most recent events I wouldn't put it past her to lie about inconvenient truths. For example, if she feels some guilt for Rin's mom going insane, I could see her pretending it never happened.

2. If Rin's mom (mentally) went somewhere else, have we seen any clues about who she is or where she ended up?
Onund asks Rin what her mother is doing right now, hinting that her present circumstances could be relevant to the story. Given the similarities with Kyoko Nagasawa, could she be one of the other girls in the upside down house? The LiL laws of genetics probably point against that - the other UDH girls have very different hair and/or eye colors from Rin. Here's the real tinfoil thought: what if her mother is Kyoko Nagasawa? Again, probably not, as I can't remember the narrators ever hinting that Kyoko could have a second daughter.

Are there any other possibilities that I'm forgetting, or are we to assume that Rin's mom exited the story completely when she "left", and wherever she is now isn't relevant?
I don't think Onund's comments tell us anything new about Rin's dad, but there was foreshadowing about him in a different event.



This is the exact same type of foreshadowing that I talked about in this post. In particular:

1. Yet again someone says that Sensei is old enough to be Rin's dad (ish). This idea has been expressed multiple times for Sana and for Rin, but not at all for any other character.

2. Rika asks what would happen if Rin were to learn that she's related to Sensei ("not much" is apparently the answer). This is very similar to stuff that has been hinted at for Sana, and I think in each case it foreshadows a future reveal that they actually are related.

These reinforce my belief that Sana and Rin have the same father, and he's somehow closely connected to Sensei. For my money, Nozomu Arakawa is still the most likely possibility.

Plus, Rin's admission that she'd still fuck Sensei even if he was her biological dad is just more evidence she's an Arakawa. That family fucking loves incest.
I also noticed something in Rin's TSS which I don't think anyone has brought up yet: while she was with Onund, they were being watched by The Orb.

(It also looks like there is a second round, black thing above and behind Rin's head, but it's not clear what.)

For now, my best guess is this is just symbolic. The Orb in Sensei Quest was a manifestation of the "dark entity" that Sensei mentally struggles with, and Rin has her own dark entity. So in Rin's TSS we have a reminder of her dark entity, represented by The Orb for thematic reasons.
When Sensei fought The Orb he was told that it was the "dark entity" inside of him. (I argued here that it's a manifestation of his despair after Sekai died in the original timeline).



The idea of a "dark entity" has also been linked to Rin, and in particular her depression.



Though more recently it might be feeding her obsession with Sensei.


An interesting thought: is her sexual obsession a new method for escaping the feelings (or lack thereof) that she used to deal with by cutting herself? I do think it's been an unusually long time since her last episode (I vaguely recall this being said in-game, but I could be imagining it). Using sex as a coping mechanism is also a classic Arakawa trait.
There could be a literal meaning to The Orb's presence, though. In addition to being Sensei's dark entity, The Orb was also "GOD", the combined trinity. It's presence here could show the users messing with Rin's mental state. Maybe they're making her unnaturally horny like they did to Sana in Chapter 3?


Including the orb, there are quite a few references to holes in Rin's TSS:
  • The Orb looks like a void of pure emptiness and in particular is the hole left by the missing "moon".
  • In it's first appearance, The Orb was accompanied by constant use of the audio file theholelol.mp3
  • The event's renders are labelled rinmeetsthehole.
  • Onund is the God of the Hole.
  • Rin ends up in the Room with Clocks after reaching into Onund's hole.
  • Rin meets Onund after being thrown into the Heavenly Pit, which the wiki claims is the sinkhole of that name that really exists in China.
On top of that, this is the same update that includes Io's expedition to explore the hole in the tunnels, which we learned is different from the sinkhole that swallowed the other school. I don't know if any of this means anything, but Selebus sure seems to have had fun with it.


The wiki claims Onund is from China and there's some Chinese text/speech in the TSS. I don't think anyone shared a translation yet, so here you go (These are also spoken as onund[1-3].mp3):

走 近 一 点 : "Come a little closer"

我 已经 长大 了 : "I have grown up" (this is according to google - I assume a more generic "I have grown" is intended)

全世界 都 会 知道 真相 : "The whole world will know the truth"
Finally, I want to say that I view HOPE's recent appearances differently than other people seem to. I would be very surprised if HPGL (HOPE, Peerless God of Light) is actually the same entity as the HOPE who showed up in the first two chapters. It's unlikely HPGL existed in that name/form before the seventh reset. And neither of the HOPEs is the genuine (original) USER1, though they both were/are trying to become a new one.

I've wanted to write about USER1 for quite a while, but it's a big undertaking since there are lots of little parts that only start to make sense when you look at the full picture. I'll probably need to do another playthrough first and I'm not sure when I'll find time for that.

spoilers.title: Rin's TSS
Rin's sister
spoilers.html:
The Rokuharas have said that Rin's dad was a "huge cheat" and may have had another family. It's fairly likely that he had other children and that someone found out about it - otherwise how would the Rokuharas know?

With that in mind, it makes a lot of sense to me that Onund's phrase "another you" refers to a half-sister of Rin. Finding out that such a person exists would be a big deal to Rin's mom, because it would also mean finding out that her "partner" isn't just unfaithful, he's been hiding a whole second family. That kind of shock could cause her to "leave" (more on this in the next section).

For those that don't know, I (and many others) believe that Rin and Sana are half-sisters. Sana is also a perfect fit for the other clues that Onund gives:
  • She's smaller than Rin.
  • She's more broken than Rin. (Understatement of the year)
  • There's something special about her that the gods want.
  • Gods who are more important than Onund have been trying to secure her favor.
Pegasus has made multiple attempts to get her to give herself to him, similar to what Onund does with Rin in her TSS. Pegasus is supposedly a Peerless One, making him important in the hierarchy of gods (although I have doubts about his legitimacy).



It's not just Pegasus; Sana said other gods have been doing the same thing, and Sekaori/USER3 seem very interested in getting her to accept any god at all.




Sana has something they want, something that's probably intrinsic to her since her mother went through the same thing when she was younger.

The only other character I can think of to fit these clues is Ami, but we haven't seen direct evidence of gods trying to gain her favor like with Sana. Add that to all of the preexisting hints of Sana's connection to Rin, and it's far more likely to be her.
